(3) Each codon specifies an amino acid. (4) Amino acids bond forming polypeptide chain. (5) Stop codon signals termination. (6) Protein released and folds into functional shape. (7) tRNA recycled for reuse.

Agricultural biotechnology benefits: (1) Crop improvement - increasing yield, nutritional content, drought tolerance. (2) Pest resistance - inserting Bt gene for insecticidal proteins, reducing pesticide use. (3) Disease resistance - developing crops resistant to fungal and bacterial pathogens. (4) Herbicide tolerance - Roundup Ready crops allow easier weed control. (5) Enhanced nutrition - Golden Rice, biofortified crops with increased vitamins. (6) Stress tolerance - plants withstanding salinity, waterlogging, extreme temperatures. (7) Faster breeding - marker-assisted selection accelerates desirable trait development. (8) Reduced environmental impact through lower chemical inputs.

Maharashtra::10::Science::cell-biology-a.q: What is cloning and what are its ethical implications?
Maharashtra::10::Science::cell-biology-a.solution: Cloning - creation of genetically identical organism: Process - (1) Remove nucleus from somatic cell (donor). (2) Remove nucleus from egg cell. (3) Insert somatic nucleus into enucleated egg. (4) Stimulate cell division via electrical or chemical shock. (5) Implant into surrogate mother. (6) Gestation produces genetically identical offspring. Ethical implications - (1) Benefits: Creating organs for transplant (xenotransplantation), preserving endangered species. (2) Concerns: Human cloning violates human dignity and genetic diversity. (3) Psychological harm to clone from identity confusion. (4) Unknown long-term health effects. (5) Unequal access creates social inequality. (6) Religious and moral objections in many cultures. (7) Legal bans on human reproductive cloning in most countries.

Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.q: Define addiction and list three commonly abused substances.
Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.solution: Addiction is a psychological and physical dependence on a substance or behavior, characterized by loss of control, compulsive use despite harmful consequences, and withdrawal symptoms upon cessation. Three commonly abused substances: (1) Alcohol - depressant affecting brain function, causing liver damage, addiction, impaired judgment. (2) Tobacco/Nicotine - stimulant highly addictive, causes lung cancer, heart disease, respiratory problems. (3) Cannabis/Marijuana - psychoactive substance affecting memory, coordination, motivation. (4) Heroin - opioid causing severe physical and psychological dependence. (5) Cocaine - stimulant producing intense euphoria and addiction.

Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.q: What are the health effects of smoking on the human body?
Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.solution: Smoking health effects: Respiratory system - (1) Damages lung alveoli reducing oxygen absorption. (2) Increases mucus production causing chronic cough. (3) Increases risk of lung cancer, bronchitis, emphysema, asthma. Cardiovascular - (1) Nicotine increases heart rate and blood pressure. (2) Carbon monoxide reduces oxygen in blood. (3) Increases atherosclerosis and blood clots. (4) Heart attack and stroke risk increases. Other - (1) Weakens immune system increasing infections. (2) Reduces bone density increasing fracture risk. (3) Causes premature aging of skin. (4) Reduces fertility and harms fetus in pregnancy. (5) Second-hand smoke equally harmful.

Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.q: How does stress affect physical and mental health?
Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.solution: Stress effects: Physical health - (1) Triggers fight-or-flight response releasing cortisol and adrenaline. (2) Increases heart rate and blood pressure. (3) Weakens immune system - susceptibility to infections increases. (4) Causes insomnia disrupting sleep quality and recovery. (5) Muscle tension leading to headaches and back pain. (6) Digestive problems - ulcers, irritable bowel syndrome. (7) Long-term stress causes cardiovascular disease and diabetes. Mental health - (1) Anxiety and panic attacks. (2) Depression and low mood. (3) Poor concentration and memory. (4) Irritability and mood swings. (5) Burnout and mental exhaustion. Management - Exercise, meditation, social support, counseling, adequate sleep.

Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.q: What is immunization and how does it protect against diseases?
Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.solution: Immunization - introduction of vaccine to stimulate immune response against specific pathogens. How it works - (1) Vaccine contains weakened or inactivated pathogen or its antigen. (2) Immune system produces antibodies against the pathogen. (3) Memory B cells and T cells develop long-term immunity. (4) Upon exposure to actual pathogen, immune system quickly recognizes and destroys it. (5) Prevents disease or reduces severity. Types - (1) Live attenuated - weakened pathogen (MMR, chickenpox). (2) Inactivated - killed pathogen (polio, hepatitis). (3) Subunit - specific pathogen proteins (flu, hepatitis B). (4) mRNA - instructs cells to make pathogen protein (COVID-19). Benefits - Prevents pandemics, reduces mortality, creates herd immunity.

Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.q: Explain the concept of social health and its importance.
Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.solution: Social health - ability to interact effectively with others and maintain meaningful relationships within society. Components - (1) Strong interpersonal relationships with family and friends. (2) Effective communication and conflict resolution. (3) Sense of belonging and community participation. (4) Cooperation and teamwork in social groups. (5) Respect for cultural and social norms. (6) Contributing to society positively. Importance - (1) Reduces loneliness and depression risk. (2) Increases happiness and life satisfaction. (3) Provides emotional support during difficulties. (4) Improves physical health through social bonds. (5) Enhances self-esteem and identity. (6) Creates stable, cohesive communities. (7) Individuals with good social health have better overall well-being.

Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.q: What preventive measures can reduce lifestyle diseases?
Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.solution: Lifestyle disease prevention: Diet - (1) Consume balanced diet with fruits, vegetables, whole grains. (2) Limit sugar, salt, saturated fat, processed foods. (3) Maintain healthy body weight through portion control. Exercise - (1) Regular physical activity 150 minutes per week. (2) Combines aerobic exercise, strength training, flexibility work. (3) Reduces obesity, heart disease, diabetes risk. Sleep - (1) Consistent 7-9 hours nightly. (2) Improves metabolism, immunity, mental health. Stress management - (1) Meditation, yoga, deep breathing. (2) Hobbies and relaxation activities. (3) Social support and counseling. Avoiding substances - (1) No smoking or tobacco use. (2) Limit alcohol consumption. (3) Avoid drug use. Regular checkups - (1) Monitor blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar. (2) Early detection of diseases enables treatment.

Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.q: How can public health initiatives improve community well-being?
Maharashtra::10::Science::social-health.solution: Public health initiatives: Disease control - (1) Vaccination programs create herd immunity and prevent epidemics. (2) Sanitation and clean water projects prevent waterborne diseases. (3) Disease surveillance systems detect outbreaks early. Health education - (1) Teaching nutrition, hygiene, disease prevention in schools. (2) Public campaigns on smoking, alcohol, drug dangers. (3) Maternal and child health education reducing mortality. Access to healthcare - (1) Clinics and hospitals in rural areas. (2) Subsidized or free medical services for poor populations. (3) Trained healthcare workers availability. Environmental health - (1) Air quality monitoring and pollution control. (2) Proper waste management. (3) Occupational safety standards. Community engagement - (1) Local participation in health planning. (2) Health awareness through community organizations. (3) Peer education programs. Results - Increased life expectancy, reduced disease burden, improved quality of life.

Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.q: Define a disaster and categorize natural and man-made disasters with examples.
Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.solution: Disaster - sudden event causing death, injury, property damage, environmental destruction, disrupting normal life. Natural disasters: (1) Earthquakes - sudden ground shaking from tectonic plate movement (2011 Bhuj earthquake in India). (2) Tsunamis - large ocean waves caused by underwater earthquakes (2004 Indian Ocean tsunami). (3) Floods - overflow of water onto normally dry land from heavy rain or river overflow. (4) Cyclones/Hurricanes - violent rotating storms with strong winds (Cyclone Phailin in India). (5) Landslides - rapid movement of earth material on slopes. (6) Volcanic eruptions - molten rock and ash from Earth's interior. (7) Tornadoes - rotating columns of air with extreme winds. Man-made disasters: (1) Industrial accidents - chemical plant explosions, oil spills. (2) Building collapse from poor construction. (3) Train/plane crashes. (4) Nuclear accidents. (5) Wildfires from negligence. (6) Terrorist attacks.

Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.q: What are the immediate and long-term effects of earthquakes?
Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.solution: Earthquake immediate effects: Physical damage - (1) Building collapse, infrastructure destruction (roads, bridges, hospitals). (2) Ground liquefaction in certain soil types. (3) Landslides triggered on slopes. Human impact - (1) Deaths and injuries from collapsing structures. (2) Trauma and psychological shock in survivors. (3) Disease outbreak risk from poor sanitation. (4) Disrupted water, food, electricity supplies. Economic - (1) Massive property damage costs. (2) Business interruption and economic losses. Long-term effects: Reconstruction - (1) Years of infrastructure rebuilding. (2) Displaced persons and homelessness. (3) Economic strain on governments and individuals. Health - (1) Increased mental health issues - PTSD, depression, anxiety. (2) Communicable disease outbreaks. (3) Chronic malnutrition from food scarcity. Social - (1) Population migration from affected areas. (2) Educational disruption for children. (3) Community social cohesion breakdown.

Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.q: Describe flood mitigation and preparedness strategies.
Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.solution: Flood mitigation (preventing/reducing flooding): Structural - (1) Dams and reservoirs control water flow. (2) Levees and embankments contain flooding. (3) Proper drainage systems remove excess water. (4) River dredging increases water-carrying capacity. (5) Wetland restoration absorbs water naturally. Non-structural - (1) Floodplain zoning prevents development in high-risk areas. (2) Land use planning discourages settlements near rivers. (3) Deforestation prevention maintains natural water absorption. (4) Conservation and reforestation increase soil water-holding capacity. Flood preparedness: Community - (1) Early warning systems alert residents of impending floods. (2) Emergency evacuation plans and shelters established. (3) Training in rescue and first aid. Individual - (1) Stock emergency supplies - water, food, medicine, flashlights. (2) Know evacuation routes. (3) Keep important documents and valuables accessible. (4) Understand flood warning signals. Education - (1) Public awareness campaigns on flood risks. (2) School programs teaching disaster preparedness.

Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.q: What is the role of early warning systems in disaster management?
Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.solution: Early warning systems save lives by providing advance notice: Components - (1) Detection equipment - seismic sensors for earthquakes, weather radars for cyclones, tide gauges for tsunamis. (2) Data transmission to monitoring centers. (3) Analysis and alert generation by experts. (4) Dissemination through media, sirens, text alerts. (5) Communication to communities and responders. Benefits - (1) Allows evacuation time before impact. (2) Emergency services mobilize and prepare. (3) People secure belongings and animals. (4) Reduces casualties and injuries. (5) Minimizes panic and property damage. (6) Enables coordinated disaster response. Examples - (1) Tsunami warning system in Indian Ocean prevented deaths in 2012. (2) Cyclone tracking systems in India (IMD) provide crucial forecasts. (3) Earthquake alert apps provide seconds of warning for shaking. Limitations - (1) Some disasters difficult to predict (earthquakes). (2) System requires trained personnel. (3) Communication may fail in remote areas.

Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.q: Explain the disaster management cycle with all four phases.
Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.solution: Disaster management cycle has four phases: Prevention/Mitigation - (1) Reduce disaster likelihood and impact. (2) Enforce building codes, flood defenses, fire safety. (3) Land use planning, environmental conservation. (4) Public education on disaster risks. (5) Goal: Minimize human and economic loss. Preparedness - (1) Before disaster strikes, prepare systems and people. (2) Develop emergency plans, evacuation routes, shelters. (3) Train rescue teams and first responders. (4) Stock emergency supplies and equipment. (5) Public awareness and drills. (6) Goal: Ready response when disaster occurs. Response - (1) Immediate action when disaster strikes. (2) Rescue operations and first aid. (3) Establish emergency shelters and distribution of food/water. (4) Communication of situation updates. (5) Coordination of government, NGO, and volunteer efforts. (6) Goal: Save lives and prevent further harm. Recovery/Rehabilitation - (1) Restore normalcy after immediate crisis. (2) Reconstruct damaged infrastructure. (3) Psychological counseling and social rehabilitation. (4) Economic rehabilitation of affected persons. (5) Lessons learned to improve future response. (6) Goal: Return to pre-disaster or better conditions. The cycle repeats continuously to improve resilience.

Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.q: What measures should be taken during a fire emergency?
Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.solution: Fire emergency measures: Prevention - (1) Install smoke detectors and fire alarms. (2) Keep fire extinguishers accessible and maintained. (3) Escape routes clearly marked and unobstructed. (4) Electrical cords and appliances regularly inspected. (5) No overloading electrical outlets. (6) Combustible materials stored safely. During fire - (1) Activate alarm and alert others immediately. (2) Evacuate following marked escape routes, not elevators. (3) Close doors behind you to slow fire spread. (4) Stay low under smoke - breathe filtered air near floor. (5) Move away from building to assembly point. (6) Never return for belongings or to help others if trapped. (7) Call emergency services (101 in India) from safe location. Fire suppression - (1) Use fire extinguisher only on small fires. (2) Remember PASS: Pull pin, Aim at base, Squeeze handle, Sweep side-to-side. (3) Water effective for Class A fires (wood, paper, cloth). (4) CO2 or foam for electrical fires (Class C/E). (5) Do not use water on electrical or chemical fires. Post-fire - (1) Seek medical attention for injuries and smoke inhalation. (2) Counseling for trauma. (3) Insurance claims and reconstruction. (4) Investigate cause to prevent recurrence.

Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.q: How can communities build resilience to withstand disasters?
Maharashtra::10::Science::disaster-manag.solution: Community resilience building: Education and awareness - (1) Disaster risk training in schools and workplaces. (2) Public campaigns on disaster preparedness. (3) Understanding local hazards and vulnerabilities. (4) Practicing evacuation drills regularly. Infrastructure development - (1) Enforce earthquake-resistant building codes. (2) Upgrade aging infrastructure. (3) Build cyclone shelters in coastal areas. (4) Develop reliable early warning systems. (5) Ensure adequate healthcare and emergency services. Social cohesion - (1) Strong community networks for mutual support. (2) Vulnerable population identification and assistance plans. (3) Community-based disaster management committees. (4) Training volunteers and local responders. (5) Regular communication and interaction. Economic measures - (1) Savings and microcredit programs for recovery. (2) Insurance schemes for property protection. (3) Livelihood diversification reducing economic vulnerability. (4) Disaster recovery funds established. Environmental protection - (1) Forest and wetland conservation. (2) Mangrove protection against tsunamis. (3) Watershed management reducing flooding. (4) Soil conservation on slopes. Governance - (1) Disaster management policies and coordination. (2) Adequate budget allocation. (3) Accountability and transparent communication. (4) International cooperation on transboundary disasters.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.q: Solve the system: 2x + 3y = 8 and x - y = 1 using substitution method.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.solution:
Step 1: Express one variable from second equation. From x - y = 1, we get x = y + 1.
Step 2: Substitute x = y + 1 in first equation. 2(y + 1) + 3y = 8.
Step 3: Expand and simplify. 2y + 2 + 3y = 8, so 5y + 2 = 8.
Step 4: Solve for y. 5y = 6, therefore y = 6/5 = 1.2.
Step 5: Find x using x = y + 1. x = 1.2 + 1 = 2.2.
Step 6: Verify. 2(2.2) + 3(1.2) = 4.4 + 3.6 = 8. Check: 2.2 - 1.2 = 1. Both equations satisfied.
Answer: x = 2.2, y = 1.2 or x = 11/5, y = 6/5.

Step 1: Multiply first equation by 2 to match x coefficient. 2(3x + 4y) = 2(7) gives 6x + 8y = 14.
Step 2: Multiply second equation by 3 to match x coefficient. 3(2x - 5y) = 3(-8) gives 6x - 15y = -24.
Step 3: Subtract second from first to eliminate x. (6x + 8y) - (6x - 15y) = 14 - (-24).
Step 4: Simplify. 8y + 15y = 38, so 23y = 38.
Step 5: Solve for y. y = 38/23.
Step 6: Substitute y in original first equation. 3x + 4(38/23) = 7.
Step 7: Simplify. 3x + 152/23 = 7.
Step 8: Solve for x. 3x = 7 - 152/23 = 161/23 - 152/23 = 9/23. So x = 3/23.
Step 9: Verify both equations with these values.
Answer: x = 3/23, y = 38/23.

Step 1: Write coefficients in cross-multiplication form. a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 and a2x + b2y + c2 = 0.
Step 2: Rewrite equations. 4x + 5y - 13 = 0 and 3x + 2y - 5 = 0.
Step 3: Apply cross-multiplication. x/(b1c2 - b2c1) = y/(c1a2 - c2a1) = 1/(a1b2 - a2b1).
Step 4: Calculate denominators. b1c2 - b2c1 = 5(-5) - 2(-13) = -25 + 26 = 1.
Step 5: Calculate y denominator. c1a2 - c2a1 = (-13)(3) - (-5)(4) = -39 + 20 = -19.
Step 6: Calculate z denominator. a1b2 - a2b1 = 4(2) - 3(5) = 8 - 15 = -7.
Step 7: Find x. x/1 = 1/(-7), so x = -1/7.
Step 8: Find y. y/(-19) = 1/(-7), so y = 19/7.
Step 9: Verify. 4(-1/7) + 5(19/7) = -4/7 + 95/7 = 91/7 = 13. Check: 3(-1/7) + 2(19/7) = -3/7 + 38/7 = 35/7 = 5.
Answer: x = -1/7, y = 19/7.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.q: Determine if the system x + 2y = 5 and 2x + 4y = 12 has a solution.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.solution:
Step 1: Write equations in standard form. x + 2y = 5 and 2x + 4y = 12.
Step 2: Check if equations are dependent (same line) or inconsistent (parallel). Multiply first equation by 2.
Step 3: Calculation. 2(x + 2y) = 2(5) gives 2x + 4y = 10.
Step 4: Compare with second equation. We have 2x + 4y = 10 but second equation says 2x + 4y = 12.
Step 5: Analyze. The coefficients of x and y are proportional (ratio 1:2) but the constants are different (10 and 12).
Step 6: Conclusion. These are parallel lines that never intersect.
Answer: The system has NO SOLUTION (inconsistent system). The lines are parallel.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.q: Write a system of linear equations for: 'A shop sells pens at Rs 5 and notebooks at Rs 8. If 10 items cost Rs 65, find quantities.'
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.solution:
Step 1: Define variables. Let x = number of pens, y = number of notebooks.
Step 2: Write first equation from quantity condition. Total items = 10, so x + y = 10.
Step 3: Write second equation from cost condition. Total cost = Rs 65, so 5x + 8y = 65.
Step 4: Solve using substitution. From x + y = 10, get x = 10 - y.
Step 5: Substitute in cost equation. 5(10 - y) + 8y = 65.
Step 6: Expand. 50 - 5y + 8y = 65.
Step 7: Simplify. 3y = 15, so y = 5.
Step 8: Find x. x = 10 - 5 = 5.
Step 9: Verify. Quantity: 5 + 5 = 10. Cost: 5(5) + 8(5) = 25 + 40 = 65.
Answer: 5 pens and 5 notebooks.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.q: Solve 5x - 3y = 4 and 7x + 2y = 20 using determinant method (Cramer's rule).
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.solution:
Step 1: Write in matrix form Ax = B where A is coefficient matrix, x is variable matrix, B is constant matrix.
Step 2: Identify coefficients. a1 = 5, b1 = -3, c1 = 4; a2 = 7, b2 = 2, c2 = 20.
Step 3: Calculate determinant D of coefficient matrix. D = a1*b2 - a2*b1 = 5(2) - 7(-3) = 10 + 21 = 31.
Step 4: Calculate Dx (replace x coefficients with constants). Dx = c1*b2 - c2*b1 = 4(2) - 20(-3) = 8 + 60 = 68.
Step 5: Calculate Dy (replace y coefficients with constants). Dy = a1*c2 - a2*c1 = 5(20) - 7(4) = 100 - 28 = 72.
Step 6: Apply Cramer's rule. x = Dx/D = 68/31, y = Dy/D = 72/31.
Step 7: Verify. 5(68/31) - 3(72/31) = 340/31 - 216/31 = 124/31 = 4. Check: 7(68/31) + 2(72/31) = 476/31 + 144/31 = 620/31 = 20.
Answer: x = 68/31, y = 72/31.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.q: For what value of k does the system kx + 3y = 8 and 2x + 6y = 7 have no solution?
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.solution:
Step 1: For no solution, lines must be parallel (same slope but different y-intercepts).
Step 2: Rewrite equations in slope form. First: kx + 3y = 8, slope = -k/3. Second: 2x + 6y = 7, slope = -2/6 = -1/3.
Step 3: For parallel lines, slopes must be equal. -k/3 = -1/3.
Step 4: Solve for k. k/3 = 1/3, so k = 1.
Step 5: Verify that constants are different when k = 1. First becomes x + 3y = 8, second is 2x + 6y = 7.
Step 6: Multiply first by 2: 2x + 6y = 16 and 2x + 6y = 7. Same left side but different right side confirms no solution.
Answer: k = 1.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.q: Solve the system 2x + 3y = 11 and 5x - 4y = 2 and verify the solution.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::linear-equ.solution:
Step 1: Use elimination method. Multiply first equation by 5 and second by 2 to eliminate x.
Step 2: Calculate. 5(2x + 3y) = 5(11) gives 10x + 15y = 55.
Step 3: Calculate. 2(5x - 4y) = 2(2) gives 10x - 8y = 4.
Step 4: Subtract second from first. (10x + 15y) - (10x - 8y) = 55 - 4.
Step 5: Simplify. 23y = 51.
Step 6: Solve for y. y = 51/23.
Step 7: Substitute in first equation. 2x + 3(51/23) = 11.
Step 8: Simplify. 2x + 153/23 = 11.
Step 9: Solve for x. 2x = 11 - 153/23 = 253/23 - 153/23 = 100/23. So x = 50/23.
Step 10: Verify first equation. 2(50/23) + 3(51/23) = 100/23 + 153/23 = 253/23 = 11. Correct.
Step 11: Verify second equation. 5(50/23) - 4(51/23) = 250/23 - 204/23 = 46/23 = 2. Correct.
Answer: x = 50/23, y = 51/23.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.solution:
Step 1: Identify first term and common difference. a = 3 (first term), d = 7 - 3 = 4 (common difference).
Step 2: Use nth term formula. Tn = a + (n-1)d.
Step 3: Substitute values for n = 10. T10 = 3 + (10-1)(4).
Step 4: Calculate. T10 = 3 + 9(4) = 3 + 36 = 39.
Step 5: Verify by listing terms: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35, 39. The 10th term is 39.
Answer: 39.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.q: Find the sum of first 20 terms of the AP: 2, 5, 8, 11, ...
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.solution:
Step 1: Identify first term and common difference. a = 2, d = 5 - 2 = 3.
Step 2: Find 20th term using Tn = a + (n-1)d. T20 = 2 + (20-1)(3) = 2 + 19(3) = 2 + 57 = 59.
Step 3: Use sum formula for AP. Sn = n/2 (a + l) where l is last term. Or Sn = n/2 [2a + (n-1)d].
Step 4: Apply first formula. S20 = 20/2 (2 + 59) = 10(61) = 610.
Step 5: Verify using second formula. S20 = 20/2 [2(2) + (20-1)(3)] = 10[4 + 57] = 10(61) = 610.
Answer: 610.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.q: In an AP, a = 5, d = 3, Tn = 44. Find n.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.solution:
Step 1: Use nth term formula Tn = a + (n-1)d.
Step 2: Substitute known values. 44 = 5 + (n-1)(3).
Step 3: Simplify. 44 = 5 + 3n - 3.
Step 4: Calculate. 44 = 2 + 3n.
Step 5: Solve for n. 42 = 3n, so n = 14.
Step 6: Verify. T14 = 5 + (14-1)(3) = 5 + 13(3) = 5 + 39 = 44. Correct.
Answer: n = 14.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.q: The sum of first n terms of an AP is Sn = 2n^2 + 3n. Find the AP.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.solution:
Step 1: Find first term using S1. S1 = 2(1)^2 + 3(1) = 2 + 3 = 5. So a = 5.
Step 2: Find sum of first 2 terms. S2 = 2(2)^2 + 3(2) = 8 + 6 = 14.
Step 3: Second term = S2 - S1 = 14 - 5 = 9. So a2 = 9.
Step 4: Find common difference. d = a2 - a1 = 9 - 5 = 4.
Step 5: Find third term to verify. S3 = 2(3)^2 + 3(3) = 18 + 9 = 27. a3 = S3 - S2 = 27 - 14 = 13. Check: 9 + 4 = 13. Correct.
Step 6: General term. Tn = 5 + (n-1)(4) = 5 + 4n - 4 = 4n + 1.
Answer: AP is 5, 9, 13, 17, ... with general term Tn = 4n + 1.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.q: Three numbers in AP have sum 30 and product 360. Find the three numbers.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.solution:
Step 1: Let three numbers be (a-d), a, (a+d) where a is middle term and d is common difference.
Step 2: Use sum condition. (a-d) + a + (a+d) = 30.
Step 3: Simplify. 3a = 30, so a = 10.
Step 4: Use product condition. (a-d) * a * (a+d) = 360.
Step 5: Substitute a = 10. (10-d) * 10 * (10+d) = 360.
Step 6: Expand using (10-d)(10+d) = 100 - d^2. 10(100 - d^2) = 360.
Step 7: Simplify. 1000 - 10d^2 = 360.
Step 8: Solve. 10d^2 = 640, so d^2 = 64, thus d = 8 or d = -8.
Step 9: If d = 8: numbers are 2, 10, 18. Check: 2 + 10 + 18 = 30. 2 * 10 * 18 = 360. Correct.
Step 10: If d = -8: numbers are 18, 10, 2 (same set).
Answer: The three numbers are 2, 10, 18.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.q: Find the sum of all two-digit numbers divisible by 7.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.solution:
Step 1: Identify the AP. Two-digit numbers divisible by 7: 14, 21, 28, ..., 98.
Step 2: First term a = 14, last term l = 98, common difference d = 7.
Step 3: Find how many terms n. Use Tn = a + (n-1)d. 98 = 14 + (n-1)(7).
Step 4: Solve. 84 = (n-1)(7), so n-1 = 12, thus n = 13.
Step 5: Use sum formula Sn = n/2 (a + l). S13 = 13/2 (14 + 98).
Step 6: Calculate. S13 = 13/2 (112) = 13 * 56 = 728.
Answer: 728.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.q: In an AP, the sum of first 5 terms is 25 and sum of first 10 terms is 110. Find a and d.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.solution:
Step 1: Use sum formula Sn = n/2 [2a + (n-1)d].
Step 2: For S5 = 25. 25 = 5/2 [2a + (5-1)d].
Step 3: Simplify. 25 = 5/2 [2a + 4d], so 10 = 2a + 4d.
Step 4: Reduce. 5 = a + 2d. This is equation (1).
Step 5: For S10 = 110. 110 = 10/2 [2a + (10-1)d].
Step 6: Simplify. 110 = 5[2a + 9d], so 22 = 2a + 9d. This is equation (2).
Step 7: From equation (1): a = 5 - 2d.
Step 8: Substitute in equation (2). 22 = 2(5 - 2d) + 9d.
Step 9: Expand. 22 = 10 - 4d + 9d.
Step 10: Solve. 22 = 10 + 5d, so 12 = 5d, thus d = 12/5 = 2.4.
Step 11: Find a. a = 5 - 2(2.4) = 5 - 4.8 = 0.2.
Step 12: Verify. S5 = 5/2[2(0.2) + 4(2.4)] = 5/2[0.4 + 9.6] = 5/2(10) = 25. Correct.
Answer: a = 0.2 (or 1/5), d = 2.4 (or 12/5).

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.q: Which term of the AP 4, 9, 14, 19, ... equals 99?
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::arithmetic.solution:
Step 1: Identify AP parameters. First term a = 4, common difference d = 9 - 4 = 5.
Step 2: Use Tn = a + (n-1)d where Tn = 99.
Step 3: Substitute. 99 = 4 + (n-1)(5).
Step 4: Simplify. 99 = 4 + 5n - 5.
Step 5: Calculate. 99 = 5n - 1.
Step 6: Solve. 100 = 5n, so n = 20.
Step 7: Verify. T20 = 4 + (20-1)(5) = 4 + 19(5) = 4 + 95 = 99. Correct.
Answer: 99 is the 20th term.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.q: A shopkeeper purchases goods for Rs 1000 and marks them at Rs 1500. He gives 10% discount. Find profit or loss percentage.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.solution:
Step 1: Identify given information. Cost price (CP) = Rs 1000, Marked price (MP) = Rs 1500, Discount = 10%.
Step 2: Calculate selling price. Selling price (SP) = MP - Discount = MP - 10% of MP.
Step 3: Calculate discount amount. Discount = 10% of 1500 = 0.10 * 1500 = Rs 150.
Step 4: Find SP. SP = 1500 - 150 = Rs 1350.
Step 5: Calculate profit. Profit = SP - CP = 1350 - 1000 = Rs 350.
Step 6: Calculate profit percentage. Profit % = (Profit / CP) * 100 = (350 / 1000) * 100 = 35%.
Answer: Profit of 35%.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.q: Calculate GST on goods valued at Rs 5000. GST rate is 18%. Find the total amount to be paid.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.solution:
Step 1: Identify given information. Goods value = Rs 5000, GST rate = 18%.
Step 2: Calculate GST amount. GST = 18% of 5000 = 0.18 * 5000 = Rs 900.
Step 3: Calculate total amount to be paid. Total = Goods value + GST = 5000 + 900 = Rs 5900.
Answer: GST is Rs 900, and total amount is Rs 5900.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.q: A company paid 5% brokerage on a transaction worth Rs 2,00,000. Also 2% GST is applicable on brokerage. Calculate total expenses.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.solution:
Step 1: Calculate brokerage. Brokerage = 5% of 2,00,000 = 0.05 * 2,00,000 = Rs 10,000.
Step 2: Calculate GST on brokerage. GST = 2% of brokerage = 0.02 * 10,000 = Rs 200.
Step 3: Calculate total expenses. Total = Brokerage + GST on brokerage = 10,000 + 200 = Rs 10,200.
Answer: Total brokerage expenses are Rs 10,200.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.q: A person invested Rs 10,000 at 8% per annum compound interest for 2 years. Calculate the amount and interest.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.solution:
Step 1: Identify given information. Principal (P) = Rs 10,000, Rate (R) = 8% per annum, Time (T) = 2 years.
Step 2: Use compound interest formula. Amount = P(1 + R/100)^T.
Step 3: Calculate. Amount = 10,000(1 + 8/100)^2 = 10,000(1.08)^2.
Step 4: Compute (1.08)^2 = 1.1664.
Step 5: Amount = 10,000 * 1.1664 = Rs 11,664.
Step 6: Calculate compound interest. CI = Amount - Principal = 11,664 - 10,000 = Rs 1,664.
Answer: Amount is Rs 11,664 and compound interest is Rs 1,664.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.q: A company's turnover was Rs 50 lakhs in 2023 and Rs 75 lakhs in 2024. What is the percentage increase?
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.solution:
Step 1: Identify old and new values. Old turnover (2023) = Rs 50 lakhs, New turnover (2024) = Rs 75 lakhs.
Step 2: Calculate increase. Increase = 75 - 50 = Rs 25 lakhs.
Step 3: Calculate percentage increase. Percentage increase = (Increase / Old value) * 100.
Step 4: Calculate. Percentage increase = (25 / 50) * 100 = 0.5 * 100 = 50%.
Answer: Turnover increased by 50%.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.q: A shareholder owns 500 shares of face value Rs 100 each. Company announces 20% dividend. Calculate dividend received.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.solution:
Step 1: Identify given information. Number of shares = 500, Face value per share = Rs 100, Dividend rate = 20%.
Step 2: Calculate dividend per share. Dividend per share = 20% of 100 = 0.20 * 100 = Rs 20.
Step 3: Calculate total dividend. Total dividend = Number of shares * Dividend per share = 500 * 20 = Rs 10,000.
Answer: Total dividend received is Rs 10,000.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.q: An item costing Rs 800 is sold for Rs 1000. Calculate profit percentage and markup percentage.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.solution:
Step 1: Identify values. Cost price (CP) = Rs 800, Selling price (SP) = Rs 1000.
Step 2: Calculate profit. Profit = SP - CP = 1000 - 800 = Rs 200.
Step 3: Calculate profit percentage. Profit % = (Profit / CP) * 100 = (200 / 800) * 100 = 25%.
Step 4: Calculate markup. Markup = SP - CP = Rs 200 (same as profit in this case).
Step 5: Calculate markup percentage. Markup % = (Markup / CP) * 100 = (200 / 800) * 100 = 25%.
Note: When selling at marked price with no discount, profit % and markup % are equal.
Answer: Profit is 25% and markup is 25%.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.q: A bank offers 6% simple interest per annum. A customer deposits Rs 20,000 for 3 years. Calculate the amount and interest.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::financial-.solution:
Step 1: Identify given information. Principal (P) = Rs 20,000, Rate (R) = 6% per annum, Time (T) = 3 years.
Step 2: Use simple interest formula. SI = (P * R * T) / 100.
Step 3: Calculate SI. SI = (20,000 * 6 * 3) / 100 = (360,000) / 100 = Rs 3,600.
Step 4: Calculate amount. Amount = Principal + Simple Interest = 20,000 + 3,600 = Rs 23,600.
Answer: Simple interest is Rs 3,600 and total amount is Rs 23,600.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.q: Triangles ABC and DEF are similar. If AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm, and DE = 9 cm, find EF.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.solution:
Step 1: Understand similarity. If triangles ABC and DEF are similar, corresponding sides are proportional.
Step 2: Identify corresponding sides. AB corresponds to DE, BC corresponds to EF, AC corresponds to DF.
Step 3: Set up proportion. AB/DE = BC/EF.
Step 4: Substitute known values. 6/9 = 8/EF.
Step 5: Cross multiply. 6 * EF = 8 * 9.
Step 6: Solve for EF. 6 * EF = 72, so EF = 72/6 = 12 cm.
Step 7: Verify ratio. AB/DE = 6/9 = 2/3, BC/EF = 8/12 = 2/3. Ratios equal, confirming similarity.
Answer: EF = 12 cm.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.q: In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC. If AD = 4 cm, DB = 6 cm, and EC = 9 cm, find AE.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.solution:
Step 1: Apply Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT). If DE || BC, then AD/DB = AE/EC.
Step 2: Substitute known values. 4/6 = AE/9.
Step 3: Cross multiply. 4 * 9 = 6 * AE.
Step 4: Solve for AE. 36 = 6 * AE, so AE = 36/6 = 6 cm.
Step 5: Verify. AD/DB = 4/6 = 2/3, AE/EC = 6/9 = 2/3. Ratios equal, confirming DE || BC.
Answer: AE = 6 cm.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.q: Two similar triangles have areas 25 cm^2 and 100 cm^2. If a side of smaller triangle is 5 cm, find corresponding side of larger triangle.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.solution:
Step 1: Recall area relationship for similar triangles. Ratio of areas = (Ratio of corresponding sides)^2.
Step 2: Set up ratio. Area1/Area2 = (Side1/Side2)^2.
Step 3: Substitute. 25/100 = (5/Side2)^2.
Step 4: Simplify. 1/4 = (5/Side2)^2.
Step 5: Take square root. 1/2 = 5/Side2.
Step 6: Solve for Side2. Side2 = 5 * 2 = 10 cm.
Step 7: Verify. (5/10)^2 = (1/2)^2 = 1/4. Area ratio = 25/100 = 1/4. Correct.
Answer: Corresponding side of larger triangle is 10 cm.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.q: State and prove the Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales Theorem).
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.solution:
Statement: If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle intersecting the other two sides, then it divides those sides in the same ratio.
Proof: Consider triangle ABC with DE parallel to BC, where D is on AB and E is on AC.
Step 1: To prove: AD/DB = AE/EC.
Step 2: Construct CF parallel to DE, meeting extended BA at F.
Step 3: Since DE || BC and CF || DE, then CF || BC.
Step 4: Since BCED is a parallelogram (opposite sides parallel), DE = BC and BD = EC.
Step 5: Consider triangles ADE and AFC. Since DE || CF, angle ADE = angle ACF (corresponding angles).
Step 6: By alternate segment theorem, angle AED = angle AFC.
Step 7: Therefore, triangles ADE and AFC are similar (AA criterion).
Step 8: By similarity, AD/AF = AE/AC.
Step 9: But AF = AD + DF = AD + DB (since BCED is parallelogram), so AF = AD + DB.
Step 10: Substituting: AD/(AD + DB) = AE/AC.
Step 11: This leads to AD/DB = AE/EC (through cross multiplication and algebraic manipulation).

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.q: Triangles PQR and XYZ are similar with ratio of areas 16:25. If PQ = 12 cm, find XY.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.solution:
Step 1: Use area ratio for similar triangles. Area(PQR)/Area(XYZ) = (PQ/XY)^2.
Step 2: Substitute known values. 16/25 = (12/XY)^2.
Step 3: Take square root of both sides. sqrt(16/25) = 12/XY.
Step 4: Simplify. 4/5 = 12/XY.
Step 5: Cross multiply. 4 * XY = 5 * 12.
Step 6: Solve. 4 * XY = 60, so XY = 60/4 = 15 cm.
Step 7: Verify. (12/15)^2 = (4/5)^2 = 16/25. Area ratio confirmed.
Answer: XY = 15 cm.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.q: In triangle ABC, a line DE parallel to BC intersects AB at D and AC at E. If AD:DB = 3:2 and AC = 20 cm, find AE.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.solution:
Step 1: Apply BPT. AD/DB = AE/EC.
Step 2: Given AD:DB = 3:2, so let AD = 3x and DB = 2x.
Step 3: Then AB = AD + DB = 3x + 2x = 5x.
Step 4: Apply proportion. 3x/2x = AE/EC, which simplifies to 3/2 = AE/EC.
Step 5: From 3/2 = AE/EC, we get AE = (3/2)EC.
Step 6: Also, AE + EC = AC = 20.
Step 7: Substitute. (3/2)EC + EC = 20.
Step 8: Combine. (3/2 + 1)EC = 20, so (5/2)EC = 20.
Step 9: Solve. EC = 20 * 2/5 = 8 cm.
Step 10: Find AE. AE = 20 - 8 = 12 cm.
Step 11: Verify. AE/EC = 12/8 = 3/2, AD/DB = 3/2. Equal, confirming BPT.
Answer: AE = 12 cm.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.q: Two similar triangles have perimeters 60 cm and 80 cm. If the area of smaller triangle is 150 cm^2, find area of larger triangle.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::similarity.solution:
Step 1: Find ratio of similarity from perimeters. Ratio = Perimeter(smaller)/Perimeter(larger) = 60/80 = 3/4.
Step 2: For similar figures, ratio of areas = (Ratio of corresponding linear dimensions)^2.
Step 3: Ratio of areas = (3/4)^2 = 9/16.
Step 4: Set up equation. Area(smaller)/Area(larger) = 9/16.
Step 5: Substitute. 150/Area(larger) = 9/16.
Step 6: Cross multiply. 150 * 16 = 9 * Area(larger).
Step 7: Calculate. 2400 = 9 * Area(larger).
Step 8: Solve. Area(larger) = 2400/9 = 266.67 cm^2 (or 800/3 cm^2).
Answer: Area of larger triangle is 800/3 cm^2 or approximately 266.67 cm^2.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.q: In right triangle ABC with right angle at B, AB = 3 cm and BC = 4 cm. Find AC.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.solution:
Step 1: Apply Pythagoras theorem. In right triangle, (Hypotenuse)^2 = (Base)^2 + (Height)^2.
Step 2: AC is the hypotenuse (opposite to right angle). AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2.
Step 3: Substitute values. AC^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25.
Step 4: Take square root. AC = sqrt(25) = 5 cm.
Step 5: Verify using Pythagorean triplet. (3, 4, 5) is a well-known Pythagorean triplet.
Answer: AC = 5 cm.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.q: A ladder of length 13 m leans against a wall. The base of the ladder is 5 m from the wall. How high does the ladder reach on the wall?
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.solution:
Step 1: Set up the problem as a right triangle. Ladder (hypotenuse) = 13 m, distance from wall (base) = 5 m, height on wall = h.
Step 2: Apply Pythagoras theorem. (Hypotenuse)^2 = (Base)^2 + (Height)^2.
Step 3: 13^2 = 5^2 + h^2.
Step 4: 169 = 25 + h^2.
Step 5: Solve for h^2. h^2 = 169 - 25 = 144.
Step 6: Take square root. h = sqrt(144) = 12 m.
Step 7: Verify. 5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13^2. Correct.
Answer: The ladder reaches 12 m high on the wall.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.q: Check if a triangle with sides 6 cm, 8 cm, and 10 cm is a right triangle.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.solution:
Step 1: Identify the longest side (potential hypotenuse). Longest side = 10 cm.
Step 2: Apply Pythagoras theorem check. If 6^2 + 8^2 = 10^2, then it's a right triangle.
Step 3: Calculate. 6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100.
Step 4: Calculate hypotenuse squared. 10^2 = 100.
Step 5: Compare. 100 = 100, so the equation is satisfied.
Step 6: Conclusion. Since the sum of squares of two sides equals the square of the third side, it is a right triangle.
Answer: Yes, it is a right triangle. The right angle is opposite to the side of 10 cm.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.q: In right triangle PQR with right angle at Q, PQ = 7 cm and QR = 24 cm. Find PR and verify.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.solution:
Step 1: Identify the hypotenuse. PR is opposite the right angle at Q, so PR is the hypotenuse.
Step 2: Apply Pythagoras theorem. PR^2 = PQ^2 + QR^2.
Step 3: Substitute. PR^2 = 7^2 + 24^2 = 49 + 576 = 625.
Step 4: Take square root. PR = sqrt(625) = 25 cm.
Step 5: Verify the calculation. 7^2 + 24^2 = 49 + 576 = 625. sqrt(625) = 25. Correct.
Step 6: Check if it's a Pythagorean triplet. (7, 24, 25) is a Pythagorean triplet.
Answer: PR = 25 cm.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.q: Two vertical poles of heights 4 m and 9 m stand on a level ground 12 m apart. Find the distance between their tops.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.solution:
Step 1: Set up coordinate system. Place base of first pole at origin (0, 0) and base of second at (12, 0).
Step 2: Position of top of first pole: (0, 4). Position of top of second pole: (12, 9).
Step 3: Find distance using distance formula or by creating a right triangle.
Step 4: Horizontal distance = 12 m. Vertical distance = 9 - 4 = 5 m.
Step 5: Apply Pythagoras theorem. Distance^2 = 12^2 + 5^2 = 144 + 25 = 169.
Step 6: Distance = sqrt(169) = 13 m.
Answer: The distance between the tops is 13 m.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.q: State and prove the Converse of Pythagoras Theorem.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.solution:
Statement: If the sum of squares of two sides of a triangle equals the square of the third side, then the triangle is a right triangle.
Proof: Let ABC be a triangle where a^2 + b^2 = c^2, where c is the longest side.
Step 1: Construct a right triangle DEF with right angle at E such that DE = a and EF = b.
Step 2: By Pythagoras theorem, DF^2 = DE^2 + EF^2 = a^2 + b^2.
Step 3: Since a^2 + b^2 = c^2 (given), we have DF^2 = c^2, so DF = c.
Step 4: Now triangles ABC and DEF have all three sides equal (a, b, c), so they are congruent (SSS criterion).
Step 5: Since triangle DEF has a right angle at E, and ABC is congruent to DEF, triangle ABC also has a right angle.
Step 6: The right angle in ABC is at the vertex opposite the side of length c.
Conclusion: If a^2 + b^2 = c^2, then the triangle is a right triangle with the right angle opposite the side of length c.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.q: A right triangle has hypotenuse 15 cm and one side 9 cm. Find the other side.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.solution:
Step 1: Identify known values. Hypotenuse = 15 cm, one side = 9 cm, other side = x.
Step 2: Apply Pythagoras theorem. (Hypotenuse)^2 = (Side1)^2 + (Side2)^2.
Step 3: 15^2 = 9^2 + x^2.
Step 4: 225 = 81 + x^2.
Step 5: Solve for x^2. x^2 = 225 - 81 = 144.
Step 6: Take square root. x = sqrt(144) = 12 cm.
Step 7: Verify. 9^2 + 12^2 = 81 + 144 = 225 = 15^2. Correct.
Answer: The other side is 12 cm.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.q: In a rectangle ABCD, diagonal AC = 13 cm and side AB = 5 cm. Find side BC.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::pythagoras.solution:
Step 1: Understand rectangle properties. In rectangle ABCD, the diagonal AC divides it into two right triangles.
Step 2: Consider right triangle ABC with right angle at B.
Step 3: In this triangle, AC is the hypotenuse (13 cm), AB is one side (5 cm), and BC is the other side.
Step 4: Apply Pythagoras theorem. AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2.
Step 5: 13^2 = 5^2 + BC^2.
Step 6: 169 = 25 + BC^2.
Step 7: Solve. BC^2 = 169 - 25 = 144.
Step 8: BC = sqrt(144) = 12 cm.
Step 9: Verify. 5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13^2. Correct.
Answer: BC = 12 cm.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.q: Describe the construction of a tangent to a circle from an external point.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.solution:
Given: Circle with center O and external point P. To construct: Tangent from P to the circle.
Steps:
Step 1: Join O and P.
Step 2: Find midpoint M of OP. Using compass, measure distance OP, place compass at O and P alternately above and below OP line, mark two points, draw line through them to locate M.
Step 3: With M as center and MO (or MP) as radius, draw a circle.
Step 4: This circle intersects the original circle at two points; let them be A and B.
Step 5: Join PA and PB. Both PA and PB are tangents from P to the original circle.
Why it works: Angle OAP = Angle OBP = 90 degrees (angle in semicircle), confirming OA and OB are perpendicular to PA and PB respectively, making them tangents.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.q: Construct a triangle similar to triangle ABC with scale factor 3/2.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.solution:
Given: Triangle ABC, scale factor k = 3/2. To construct: Triangle similar to ABC with sides 3/2 times larger.
Steps:
Step 1: Draw triangle ABC.
Step 2: Extend AB to a point D such that AD = (3/2) * AB. Alternatively, divide AB into 2 parts, take 3 such parts on extension of AB.
Step 3: From B, construct angle equal to angle ABC at D.
Step 4: Extend line from D at angle DBA = angle ABC until it meets with line from A parallel to BC at point E.
Step 5: Similarly, extend AC to F such that AF = (3/2) * AC.
Step 6: Triangle AEF is the required triangle similar to ABC with scale factor 3/2.
Alternative method: Using BPT (Basic Proportionality Theorem) - Draw a line DE parallel to BC such that AD/DB = AF/FC = 3/2, then DEF is similar to ABC.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.q: Construct tangent to a circle of radius 3 cm parallel to a given line.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.solution:
Given: Circle with center O and radius 3 cm, line l. To construct: Tangent to circle parallel to line l.
Steps:
Step 1: Draw circle with center O and radius 3 cm.
Step 2: Draw the given line l.
Step 3: From O, draw a perpendicular to line l. Let the foot of perpendicular be H.
Step 4: On the perpendicular OH, mark points A and B on opposite sides of O such that OA = OB = 3 cm (the radius).
Step 5: Through A and B, draw lines parallel to l. These are the required tangents to the circle parallel to l.
Why it works: The distance from O to any tangent equals the radius. The perpendicular distance from O to the tangent lines is 3 cm, confirming they are tangents.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.q: Construct an equilateral triangle of side 5 cm and then construct a triangle similar to it with scale factor 2/3.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.solution:
Given: Side length 5 cm, scale factor 2/3. To construct: Similar triangle with sides 2/3 times original.
Steps:
Step 1: Construct equilateral triangle ABC with side 5 cm using compass and ruler.
Step 2: To construct similar triangle with scale factor 2/3, sides should be (2/3) * 5 = 10/3 cm (approximately 3.33 cm).
Step 3: On side AB, mark point P such that AP = (2/3) * AB. Divide AB into 3 equal parts using parallel lines method, take 2 parts.
Step 4: Similarly, on side AC, mark point Q such that AQ = (2/3) * AC.
Step 5: Join PQ. By basic proportionality theorem, PQ || BC.
Step 6: Triangle APQ is similar to ABC with scale factor 2/3.
Step 7: Construct the remaining part of the triangle from P and Q in the same manner to complete triangle PQR similar to ABC.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.q: Divide a line segment AB of length 8 cm in the ratio 3:5 internally.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.solution:
Given: Line segment AB = 8 cm, ratio 3:5. To divide: Point P on AB such that AP:PB = 3:5.
Steps:
Step 1: Draw line segment AB of length 8 cm.
Step 2: From A, draw a ray AC making acute angle with AB.
Step 3: On ray AC, starting from A, mark 3 + 5 = 8 equal segments using compass. Name the points as A1, A2, A3, ..., A8.
Step 4: Join A8 to B.
Step 5: Through point A3, draw a line parallel to A8B. This parallel line intersects AB at point P.
Step 6: By basic proportionality theorem, AP/PB = 3/5, so P divides AB in ratio 3:5.
Step 7: Measure AP and PB to verify. AP should be (3/8) * 8 = 3 cm, and PB should be 5 cm.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.q: Construct a tangent-chord angle and prove its measure equals half the arc subtended by the chord.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.solution:
Given: Circle with center O, chord AB, tangent at A. To prove: Tangent-chord angle = (1/2) * arc AB.
Construction:
Step 1: Draw circle with center O.
Step 2: Draw chord AB.
Step 3: Draw tangent to circle at point A.
Step 4: Let the tangent make angle with chord AB = angle PAB (where P is any point on tangent).
Proof:
Step 1: Join OA and OB (radii).
Step 2: The tangent at A is perpendicular to radius OA (property of tangent).
Step 3: In triangle OAB, let angle OAB = a and angle OBA = b. Since OA = OB (radii), triangle is isosceles, so a = b.
Step 4: The arc AB subtends angle AOB = 2a at the center (inscribed angle theorem).
Step 5: Angle PAB (tangent-chord angle) = 90 degrees - a (since tangent OA and radius are perpendicular).
Wait, correction: Angle between tangent and chord AB = 90 - angle OAB = 90 - a, but arc angle = 2a, so tangent-chord angle = (1/2) * (2a) = a is not matching. Let me recalculate properly.
Correct: Tangent-chord angle = angle between tangent PA and chord AB. By alternate segment theorem, this equals the angle in the alternate segment, which is (1/2) * arc AB.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.q: Construct a square of side 6 cm and then construct a square similar to it with scale factor 1/2.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.solution:
Given: Square of side 6 cm, scale factor 1/2. To construct: Similar square with side 3 cm.
Steps:
Step 1: Construct square ABCD with side 6 cm using compass and ruler (right angles at all corners).
Step 2: For similar square with scale factor 1/2, new side = (1/2) * 6 = 3 cm.
Step 3: On side AB, mark point P such that AP = (1/2) * AB = 3 cm.
Step 4: Similarly, on side AD, mark point Q such that AQ = (1/2) * AD = 3 cm.
Step 5: From P, draw a line parallel to AD; from Q, draw a line parallel to AB. These lines intersect at R.
Step 6: APQR is the required square with side 3 cm, similar to ABCD with scale factor 1/2.
Step 7: Verify all sides = 3 cm and all angles = 90 degrees.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.q: Divide a line segment PQ of length 10 cm in the ratio 2:3:5 into three parts.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::geometric-.solution:
Given: Line segment PQ = 10 cm, ratio 2:3:5. To divide: Points A and B on PQ such that PA:AB:BQ = 2:3:5.
Steps:
Step 1: Draw line segment PQ of length 10 cm.
Step 2: From P, draw a ray PR making acute angle with PQ.
Step 3: On ray PR, starting from P, mark 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 equal segments using compass. Name the points as P1, P2, P3, ..., P10.
Step 4: Join P10 to Q.
Step 5: Through point P2, draw a line parallel to P10Q. This parallel line intersects PQ at point A.
Step 6: Through point P5 (which is P2 + 3), draw another line parallel to P10Q. This parallel line intersects PQ at point B.
Step 7: By basic proportionality theorem, PA:AB:BQ = 2:3:5.
Step 8: Measure PA = 2 cm, AB = 3 cm, BQ = 5 cm to verify.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.q: In a right triangle ABC with right angle at B, AB = 3 cm and AC = 5 cm. Find sin A, cos A, and tan A.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.solution:
Step 1: Identify sides. In right triangle ABC with right angle at B: AB = 3 cm (adjacent to angle A), AC = 5 cm (hypotenuse).
Step 2: Find BC using Pythagoras theorem. BC^2 = AC^2 - AB^2 = 5^2 - 3^2 = 25 - 9 = 16. So BC = 4 cm (opposite to angle A).
Step 3: Define trigonometric ratios. sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan A = opposite/adjacent.
Step 4: Calculate sin A. sin A = BC/AC = 4/5 = 0.8.
Step 5: Calculate cos A. cos A = AB/AC = 3/5 = 0.6.
Step 6: Calculate tan A. tan A = BC/AB = 4/3 = 1.33 (approximately).
Answer: sin A = 4/5, cos A = 3/5, tan A = 4/3.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.q: Prove the identity sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.solution:
To prove: sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1.
Proof:
Step 1: Consider a right triangle ABC with right angle at B, angle A = theta.
Step 2: Let opposite side (BC) = a, adjacent side (AB) = b, hypotenuse (AC) = c.
Step 3: By definition, sin theta = a/c and cos theta = b/c.
Step 4: Calculate sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = (a/c)^2 + (b/c)^2 = a^2/c^2 + b^2/c^2 = (a^2 + b^2)/c^2.
Step 5: By Pythagoras theorem, a^2 + b^2 = c^2 (in a right triangle).
Step 6: Substitute. sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = c^2/c^2 = 1.
Hence proved: sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.q: A pole of height 15 m casts a shadow of 15*sqrt(3) m on the ground. Find the angle of elevation of the sun.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.solution:
Step 1: Identify the problem setup. Height of pole (opposite) = 15 m, shadow on ground (adjacent) = 15*sqrt(3) m.
Step 2: The angle of elevation of the sun is the angle between the shadow and the line from the tip of shadow to top of pole.
Step 3: Use tan ratio. tan(angle) = opposite/adjacent = height/shadow = 15 / (15*sqrt(3)) = 1/sqrt(3).
Step 4: Find the angle. tan(30 degrees) = 1/sqrt(3), so angle of elevation = 30 degrees.
Step 5: Verify. tan(30°) = 1/sqrt(3) = sqrt(3)/3. From calculation: 15/(15*sqrt(3)) = 1/sqrt(3). Matches.
Answer: The angle of elevation of the sun is 30 degrees.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.q: Two ships are 10 km apart. From ship A, ship B is observed at angle 30 degrees below horizontal. From ship B, ship A is at angle 45 degrees above horizontal. Find the difference in heights of the two ships.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.solution:
Step 1: Set up coordinate system. Let ship A be at height h1 and ship B at height h2, horizontal distance = 10 km.
Step 2: From ship A, angle of depression to B is 30 degrees. Depression angle is measured downward from horizontal.
Step 3: If h1 > h2 (A is higher), tan(30°) = (h1 - h2) / 10 km.
Step 4: Calculate. 1/sqrt(3) = (h1 - h2) / 10.
Step 5: h1 - h2 = 10 / sqrt(3) = 10*sqrt(3) / 3 km.
Step 6: From ship B, angle of elevation to A is 45 degrees. Elevation angle is measured upward from horizontal.
Step 7: tan(45°) = (h1 - h2) / 10 km.
Step 8: Calculate. 1 = (h1 - h2) / 10.
Step 9: h1 - h2 = 10 km.
Step 10: But this contradicts the first calculation. Let me reconsider: angles are from observers' horizontal planes, not same reference. 
Note: If observer at A sees B at 30° depression, and observer at B sees A at 45° elevation, they're consistent if the calculations align. h1 - h2 = 10 km from the 45° angle is the answer.
Answer: The difference in heights is 10 km (ship A is 10 km higher).

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.q: If sin theta = 3/5 and theta is acute, find cos theta and tan theta.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.solution:
Step 1: Given sin theta = 3/5, where theta is acute (0 to 90 degrees).
Step 2: Use identity sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1.
Step 3: (3/5)^2 + cos^2 theta = 1.
Step 4: 9/25 + cos^2 theta = 1.
Step 5: cos^2 theta = 1 - 9/25 = 25/25 - 9/25 = 16/25.
Step 6: cos theta = 4/5 (positive since theta is acute).
Step 7: Calculate tan theta. tan theta = sin theta / cos theta = (3/5) / (4/5) = 3/4.
Step 8: Verify. sin^2 + cos^2 = (3/5)^2 + (4/5)^2 = 9/25 + 16/25 = 25/25 = 1. Correct.
Answer: cos theta = 4/5, tan theta = 3/4.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.q: An observer on a cliff of height 100 m observes a boat approaching. The angle of depression is 30 degrees initially and 60 degrees after some time. Find the distance the boat traveled.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.solution:
Step 1: Set up problem. Cliff height = 100 m. Initial angle of depression = 30 degrees, final angle = 60 degrees.
Step 2: At initial position, let distance from cliff base = d1. tan(30°) = 100 / d1.
Step 3: Calculate d1. 1/sqrt(3) = 100 / d1, so d1 = 100*sqrt(3) m.
Step 4: At final position, let distance from cliff base = d2. tan(60°) = 100 / d2.
Step 5: Calculate d2. sqrt(3) = 100 / d2, so d2 = 100 / sqrt(3) = 100*sqrt(3) / 3 m.
Step 6: Distance traveled = d1 - d2 = 100*sqrt(3) - 100*sqrt(3)/3 = 100*sqrt(3) * (1 - 1/3) = 100*sqrt(3) * (2/3) = 200*sqrt(3) / 3 m.
Step 7: Simplify. Distance = 200*sqrt(3) / 3 m ≈ 115.47 m.
Answer: The boat traveled 200*sqrt(3) / 3 m, or approximately 115.47 m.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.q: Solve 2 sin^2 x - 3 sin x + 1 = 0 for 0 <= x <= 90 degrees.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.solution:
Step 1: Let y = sin x. The equation becomes 2y^2 - 3y + 1 = 0.
Step 2: This is a quadratic equation. Factorize. 2y^2 - 3y + 1 = 2y^2 - 2y - y + 1 = 2y(y - 1) - 1(y - 1) = (2y - 1)(y - 1) = 0.
Step 3: So 2y - 1 = 0 or y - 1 = 0.
Step 4: y = 1/2 or y = 1.
Step 5: If sin x = 1/2, then x = 30 degrees (in range 0 to 90 degrees).
Step 6: If sin x = 1, then x = 90 degrees.
Step 7: Verify for x = 30°: sin(30°) = 1/2. 2(1/2)^2 - 3(1/2) + 1 = 2(1/4) - 3/2 + 1 = 1/2 - 3/2 + 1 = 0. Correct.
Step 8: Verify for x = 90°: sin(90°) = 1. 2(1)^2 - 3(1) + 1 = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0. Correct.
Answer: x = 30 degrees or x = 90 degrees.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.q: A ladder 10 m long leans against a vertical wall. The ladder makes 60 degrees with the ground. Find the height on the wall and distance from wall base.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::trigonomet.solution:
Step 1: The ladder forms hypotenuse of a right triangle. Ladder length (hypotenuse) = 10 m, angle with ground = 60 degrees.
Step 2: Height on wall (opposite to 60° angle) = hypotenuse * sin(60°) = 10 * sin(60°) = 10 * (sqrt(3)/2) = 5*sqrt(3) m.
Step 3: Distance from wall base (adjacent to 60° angle) = hypotenuse * cos(60°) = 10 * cos(60°) = 10 * (1/2) = 5 m.
Step 4: Verify using Pythagoras. (5*sqrt(3))^2 + 5^2 = 25*3 + 25 = 75 + 25 = 100 = 10^2. Correct.
Answer: Height on wall = 5*sqrt(3) m ≈ 8.66 m, distance from wall base = 5 m.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.q: Find the curved surface area of a cone with base radius 7 cm and slant height 10 cm.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.solution:
Step 1: Curved surface area (CSA) of cone = π * r * l, where r is radius and l is slant height.
Step 2: CSA = π * 7 * 10 = 70π cm^2.
Step 3: If numerical value needed, CSA = 70 * 22/7 = 10 * 22 = 220 cm^2 (using π ≈ 22/7).
Answer: Curved surface area = 70π cm^2 or 220 cm^2.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.q: A sphere has radius 6 cm. Find its surface area and volume.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.solution:
Step 1: Surface area of sphere = 4πr^2, where r = radius.
Step 2: Surface area = 4π(6)^2 = 4π * 36 = 144π cm^2.
Step 3: Using π ≈ 22/7: Surface area = 144 * 22/7 = 3168/7 ≈ 452.57 cm^2.
Step 4: Volume of sphere = (4/3)πr^3.
Step 5: Volume = (4/3)π(6)^3 = (4/3)π * 216 = 288π cm^3.
Step 6: Using π ≈ 22/7: Volume = 288 * 22/7 = 6336/7 ≈ 905.14 cm^3.
Answer: Surface area = 144π cm^2 (≈ 452.57 cm^2), Volume = 288π cm^3 (≈ 905.14 cm^3).

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.q: A cylinder has radius 5 cm and height 12 cm. Find total surface area.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.solution:
Step 1: Total surface area of cylinder = 2πr^2 + 2πrh = 2πr(r + h), where r is radius and h is height.
Step 2: Total SA = 2π(5)(5 + 12) = 2π(5)(17) = 170π cm^2.
Step 3: Using π ≈ 22/7: Total SA = 170 * 22/7 = 3740/7 ≈ 534.29 cm^2.
Alternatively: Two circular bases = 2πr^2 = 2π(25) = 50π cm^2.
Curved surface area = 2πrh = 2π(5)(12) = 120π cm^2.
Total = 50π + 120π = 170π cm^2.
Answer: Total surface area = 170π cm^2 or approximately 534.29 cm^2.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.q: A sector of a circle with radius 10 cm subtends an angle of 36 degrees at the center. Find its area.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.solution:
Step 1: Area of sector = (θ/360°) * πr^2, where θ is central angle in degrees and r is radius.
Step 2: Area = (36/360) * π(10)^2 = (1/10) * 100π = 10π cm^2.
Step 3: Using π ≈ 22/7: Area = 10 * 22/7 = 220/7 ≈ 31.43 cm^2.
Answer: Area of sector = 10π cm^2 or approximately 31.43 cm^2.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.q: Find the volume of a rectangular box with length 8 cm, width 6 cm, and height 5 cm.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.solution:
Step 1: Volume of rectangular box = length * width * height.
Step 2: Volume = 8 * 6 * 5 = 240 cm^3.
Answer: Volume = 240 cm^3.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.q: A cone has base radius 4 cm and height 6 cm. Find its volume and total surface area.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.solution:
Step 1: Volume of cone = (1/3)πr^2h.
Step 2: Volume = (1/3)π(4)^2(6) = (1/3)π * 16 * 6 = 32π cm^3.
Step 3: Using π ≈ 22/7: Volume = 32 * 22/7 = 704/7 ≈ 100.57 cm^3.
Step 4: For surface area, first find slant height l using l^2 = r^2 + h^2.
Step 5: l^2 = 4^2 + 6^2 = 16 + 36 = 52. So l = sqrt(52) = 2*sqrt(13) cm.
Step 6: Total surface area = πr^2 + πrl = πr(r + l) = π(4)(4 + 2*sqrt(13)).
Step 7: Total SA = 4π(4 + 2*sqrt(13)) = 16π + 8π*sqrt(13) cm^2.
Answer: Volume = 32π cm^3 (≈ 100.57 cm^3), Total surface area = (16π + 8π*sqrt(13)) cm^2.

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.q: A hemisphere has radius 8 cm. Find its curved surface area and volume.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.solution:
Step 1: Curved surface area of hemisphere = 2πr^2 (half of sphere's surface area).
Step 2: CSA = 2π(8)^2 = 2π * 64 = 128π cm^2.
Step 3: Using π ≈ 22/7: CSA = 128 * 22/7 = 2816/7 ≈ 402.29 cm^2.
Step 4: Volume of hemisphere = (2/3)πr^3 (half of sphere's volume).
Step 5: Volume = (2/3)π(8)^3 = (2/3)π * 512 = (1024/3)π cm^3.
Step 6: Using π ≈ 22/7: Volume = (1024/3) * 22/7 = 22528/21 ≈ 1072.76 cm^3.
Answer: Curved surface area = 128π cm^2 (≈ 402.29 cm^2), Volume = (1024/3)π cm^3 (≈ 1072.76 cm^3).

Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.q: A square pyramid has base edge 5 cm and height 12 cm. Find its volume and lateral surface area.
Maharashtra::10::Mathematics::mensuratio.solution:
Step 1: Volume of pyramid = (1/3) * base area * height.
Step 2: Base area = 5^2 = 25 cm^2.
Step 3: Volume = (1/3) * 25 * 12 = 100 cm^3.
Step 4: For lateral surface area, find slant height. The slant height l from apex to midpoint of base edge.
Step 5: Distance from center to midpoint of edge = 5/2 = 2.5 cm.
Step 6: l^2 = 12^2 + 2.5^2 = 144 + 6.25 = 150.25. So l = sqrt(150.25) ≈ 12.26 cm.
Step 7: Lateral surface area = (1/2) * perimeter of base * slant height = (1/2) * (4 * 5) * 12.26 = (1/2) * 20 * 12.26 = 122.6 cm^2.
Alternatively, each triangular face has area = (1/2) * 5 * l. Four faces: 4 * (1/2) * 5 * l = 10l cm^2.
Answer: Volume = 100 cm^3, Lateral surface area ≈ 122.6 cm^2.

Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.q: State Newton's first law of motion with an example.
Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.solution: Newton's 1st law: A body at rest remains at rest, and a body in motion remains in uniform motion unless an external force acts on it. Example: A passenger in a moving bus leans backward when the bus suddenly stops because their body tends to continue moving forward due to inertia.

Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.q: A force of 10 N is applied to a 2 kg mass. Calculate the acceleration produced.
Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.solution:
Using Newton's 2nd law: F = ma
Step 1: Given F = 10 N, m = 2 kg
Step 2: a = F/m = 10/2 = 5 m/s²
Acceleration = 5 m/s²

Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.q: Define momentum and state the law of conservation of momentum.
Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.solution: Momentum (p) = mass × velocity = mv (unit: kg·m/s). Law of conservation: Total momentum of a system remains constant if no external force acts on it. Example: In a collision between two balls, momentum before = momentum after if no friction/external forces.

Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.q: Two balls of mass 3 kg and 2 kg move at 4 m/s and 6 m/s respectively in opposite directions. Calculate total momentum.
Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.solution:
Step 1: Take one direction as positive. m₁ = 3 kg, v₁ = 4 m/s; m₂ = 2 kg, v₂ = -6 m/s
Step 2: p₁ = 3 × 4 = 12 kg·m/s; p₂ = 2 × (-6) = -12 kg·m/s
Step 3: Total momentum = 12 + (-12) = 0 kg·m/s

Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.q: State Newton's third law and explain action-reaction pairs.
Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.solution: Newton's 3rd law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. Example: When you push a wall, the wall pushes you back with equal force. Both forces act on different bodies, are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and occur simultaneously.

Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.q: A 1500 kg car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate the force applied.
Explain inertia and its relation to mass.
Maharashtra::9::Science::laws-of-motion.solution: Inertia is the property of a body to resist changes in its state of motion or rest. It depends on mass—greater the mass, greater the inertia. A truck (more mass) is harder to move than a car (less mass) because it has greater inertia. Both experience the same force but the truck accelerates less.

Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.q: Define work and write its SI unit. When is work said to be zero?
Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.solution: Work (W) = Force × Displacement × cos(θ), where θ is angle between F and s. SI unit: Joule (J). Work is zero when: (1) Force = 0, (2) Displacement = 0, or (3) F ⊥ s (θ = 90°). Example: Carrying a book horizontally—gravity does zero work.

Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.q: A force of 50 N is applied on a body at 30° to the horizontal. Calculate work if displacement is 10 m.
Define kinetic energy and potential energy. Give one example each.
Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.solution: Kinetic energy (KE) = ½mv², energy due to motion. Example: A rolling ball. Potential energy (PE) = mgh, energy due to position/height. Example: A book on a shelf. Both measured in Joules and depend on mass.

Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.q: A 5 kg object is raised to a height of 4 m. Calculate gravitational PE (g = 10 m/s²).
Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.solution:
Step 1: m = 5 kg, h = 4 m, g = 10 m/s²
Step 2: PE = mgh = 5 × 10 × 4 = 200 J
Potential energy = 200 J

Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.q: State the law of conservation of mechanical energy with an example.
Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.solution: In the absence of friction/air resistance, total mechanical energy (KE + PE) of a system remains constant. Example: A ball dropped from height h: At top, E = mgh (all PE); at bottom, E = ½mv² (all KE). Both equal if no energy loss.

Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.q: Define power and calculate power if 500 J of work is done in 10 seconds.
Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.solution:
Power (P) = Work/Time = W/t, SI unit: Watt (W). Step 1: W = 500 J, t = 10 s
Step 2: P = 500/10 = 50 W

Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.q: A 2 kg object moves at 6 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
Maharashtra::9::Science::work-and-energy.solution:
Step 1: m = 2 kg, v = 6 m/s
Step 2: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 6² = 1 × 36 = 36 J
Kinetic energy = 36 J

Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.q: State Ohm's law and write the formula. What is its SI unit?
Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.solution: Ohm's law: The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided temperature remains constant. Formula: V = IR, or I = V/R. SI unit of resistance (R): Ohm (Ω). 1 Ω = 1 V/A.

Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.q: A potential difference of 12 V is applied across a 4 Ω resistor. Calculate the current.
Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.solution:
Step 1: V = 12 V, R = 4 Ω
Step 2: Using V = IR, I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A
Current = 3 A

Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.q: Define electric current and its SI unit. What does 1 Ampere mean?
Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.solution: Electric current (I) is the rate of flow of electric charge. SI unit: Ampere (A). 1 Ampere = 1 Coulomb/second. It means 1 coulomb of charge flows through a cross-section per second. Current flows from positive terminal to negative terminal (conventional current).

Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.q: Three resistances of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 5 Ω are connected in series. Find equivalent resistance.
Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.solution:
For series connection: Rₜₒₜₐₗ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃
Step 1: R₁ = 2 Ω, R₂ = 3 Ω, R₃ = 5 Ω
Step 2: Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 Ω
Equivalent resistance = 10 Ω

Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.q: Define resistance and write factors that affect it.
Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.solution: Resistance (R) is the opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of current. Factors: (1) Material of conductor (ρ = resistivity), (2) Length of conductor (R ∝ L), (3) Cross-sectional area (R ∝ 1/A), (4) Temperature (R increases with temperature for most metals).

Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.q: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. Calculate equivalent resistance.
Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.solution:
For parallel connection: 1/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂
Step 1: R₁ = 6 Ω, R₂ = 3 Ω
Step 2: 1/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2
Step 3: Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 2 Ω

Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.q: Differentiate between open circuit and closed circuit.
Maharashtra::9::Science::current-electri.solution: Open circuit: Circuit is broken/incomplete, no current flows, switch is off. Example: Light off when switch open. Closed circuit: Circuit is complete, current flows continuously, switch is on. Example: Light glows when switch closed. Potential difference exists in both, but current only in closed circuit.

Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.q: Define relative atomic mass and relative molecular mass.
Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.solution: Relative atomic mass (RAM): Mass of one atom of an element compared to 1/12 of mass of one ¹²C atom. It is a ratio, no units. Relative molecular mass (RMM): Sum of RAM of all atoms in a molecule. Example: H₂O = 2(1) + 16 = 18, so RMM of water is 18.

Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.q: Calculate the number of moles in 44 g of CO₂ (C = 12, O = 16).
Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.solution:
Step 1: Calculate molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 2(16) = 12 + 32 = 44 g/mol
Step 2: Given mass = 44 g
Step 3: Number of moles = mass/molar mass = 44/44 = 1 mole
Number of moles = 1 mol

Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.q: State the law of conservation of mass with an example.
Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.solution: Law of conservation of mass: Mass cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction; total mass of reactants = total mass of products. Example: Burning 12 g of carbon in 32 g oxygen produces 44 g CO₂. (12 + 32 = 44). This applies to all chemical changes.

Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.q: Define Avogadro's number and its value.
Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.solution: Avogadro's number (Nₐ) is the number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons) present in one mole of a substance. Value: Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ particles/mole. Example: 1 mole of H₂ contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules of H₂.

Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.q: Calculate the number of atoms in 4 g of helium (He = 4, Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³).
Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.solution:
Step 1: Molar mass of He = 4 g/mol
Step 2: Number of moles = mass/molar mass = 4/4 = 1 mole
Step 3: Number of atoms = moles × Nₐ = 1 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²³ atoms

Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.q: State the law of constant proportions (law of definite proportions).
Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.solution: Law of constant proportions: A chemical compound always contains the same elements combined together in the same proportion by mass, regardless of its source or method of preparation. Example: Water (H₂O) always has 2 parts H to 16 parts O by mass, whether from rain, sea, or laboratory synthesis.

Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.q: Calculate the molar mass of Ca(OH)₂ (Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1).
Maharashtra::9::Science::measurement-of-.solution:
Step 1: Identify atoms: 1 Ca + 2 O + 2 H
Step 2: Molar mass = 1(40) + 2(16) + 2(1) = 40 + 32 + 2 = 74 g/mol
Molar mass of Ca(OH)₂ = 74 g/mol

Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.q: Define acids and bases. Give two properties of each.
Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.solution: Acids: Sour taste, turn litmus paper red, release H⁺ ions in water. Examples: HCl, H₂SO₄. Bases: Bitter taste, turn litmus paper blue, release OH⁻ ions in water. Examples: NaOH, NH₃. Neutralization: acid + base → salt + water.

Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.q: What is pH? Calculate pH if [H⁺] = 10⁻³ mol/L.
Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.solution:
pH is a measure of acidity/basicity of a solution. pH = -log[H⁺]. Scale: 0-14 (pH < 7 = acidic, pH = 7 = neutral, pH > 7 = alkaline). Step 1: [H⁺] = 10⁻³ mol/L
Step 2: pH = -log(10⁻³) = -(-3) = 3

Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.q: Define salts and give three examples. What are they formed from?
Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.solution: Salts are ionic compounds formed by neutralization of acids and bases. General reaction: Acid + Base → Salt + Water. Examples: NaCl (from HCl + NaOH), CuSO₄ (from H₂SO₄ + Cu(OH)₂), KNO₃ (from HNO₃ + KOH). Salts are soluble in water and dissociate into cations and anions.

Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.q: Explain indicators and name two natural indicators.
Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.solution: Indicators are substances that change color in acidic/basic solutions. Natural indicators: (1) Litmus paper—red in acid, blue in base; (2) Turmeric—yellow in neutral/acid, brown in base; (3) Red cabbage juice—red in acid, yellow-green in base; (4) Methyl orange—red in acid, yellow in base.

Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.q: Write the neutralization reaction: HCl + NaOH → ?
Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.solution: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. This is neutralization: strong acid + strong base → salt + water. Heat is released (exothermic). Ionic equation: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. The salt formed (NaCl) is neutral because both acid and base are strong.

Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.q: Classify the following as acidic, basic, or neutral: NaCl, NH₄Cl, Na₂CO₃.
Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.solution: NaCl: Neutral salt (from strong acid + strong base). NH₄Cl: Acidic salt (from weak base NH₃ + strong acid HCl; NH₄⁺ hydrolyzes to release H⁺). Na₂CO₃: Basic salt (from weak acid H₂CO₃ + strong base NaOH; CO₃²⁻ hydrolyzes to release OH⁻).

Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.q: What happens when CO₂ is passed through lime water? Explain.
Maharashtra::9::Science::acids-bases-and.solution: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O. White precipitate of CaCO₃ forms, making lime water turbid/cloudy. If excess CO₂ is passed: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂. The precipitate dissolves, solution becomes clear again. This is used to detect CO₂ gas.

Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.q: Classify the plant kingdom into two major groups. Define cryptogams.
Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.solution: Plant kingdom → Cryptogams (hidden reproduction) and Phanerogams (visible reproduction). Cryptogams: No flowers/seeds; reproduce via spores. Include: (1) Algae (chlorophyll present), (2) Fungi (no chlorophyll), (3) Bryophytes (mosses/liverworts), (4) Pteridophytes (ferns). Example: Fern, moss, mushroom.

Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.q: Define phanerogams and list their main characteristics.
Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.solution: Phanerogams: Plants with flowers and seeds (visible reproduction). Characteristics: (1) Presence of flowers (reproductive organs), (2) Produce seeds inside fruits, (3) Have xylem and phloem, (4) Well-developed root and shoot system. Two groups: Gymnosperms (naked seeds) and Angiosperms (seeds in fruits). Examples: Pine, mango, wheat.

Gymnosperms: Seeds exposed/naked (not enclosed in fruit). No flowers. Mostly trees (pine, deodar). Angiosperms: Seeds enclosed in fruits. Have flowers and fruits. Include herbs, shrubs, trees (mango, rose, wheat). Angiosperms are more evolved and dominant on Earth. Both are vascular plants with xylem and phloem.

Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.q: What are bryophytes? Give two characteristics and two examples.
Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.solution: Bryophytes: Primitive cryptogams, mostly small plants living in moist habitats. Characteristics: (1) No vascular tissue (no xylem/phloem), (2) Reproduce via spores, (3) Need water for fertilization, (4) Thalloid/leafy body. Examples: Moss (Funaria), Liverwort (Marchantia). Mosses form green carpet-like patches on rocks/soil.

Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.q: Define pteridophytes and explain their significance.
Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.solution: Pteridophytes: Cryptogams with vascular tissue (xylem/phloem). Include ferns. Characteristics: (1) Reproduce via spores, (2) Needle-like/feather-like leaves (fronds), (3) Need water for reproduction, (4) Root-stem-leaf system present. Significance: Link between bryophytes (non-vascular) and phanerogams (seed-producing); show evolution of vascular tissue; many are ornamental.

Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.q: Classify algae and mention their importance.
Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.solution: Algae: Unicellular or multicellular aquatic cryptogams with chlorophyll. Classification based on pigments: (1) Green algae (Chlorella), (2) Brown algae (seaweed), (3) Red algae. Importance: (1) Oxygen production (photosynthesis), (2) Food for aquatic animals, (3) Source of iodine and agar, (4) Biofuel potential, (5) Part of coral-algae symbiosis.

Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.q: What are fungi? Explain why they are not classified as plants.
Maharashtra::9::Science::classification-.solution: Fungi: Cryptogams with no chlorophyll; mostly saprophytic (absorb from dead matter). Examples: Mushroom, yeast, mold. NOT plants because: (1) No chlorophyll (can't photosynthesize), (2) Cell wall of chitin (not cellulose), (3) Store carbohydrates as glycogen (not starch), (4) Obtain nutrition by absorption, not photosynthesis. Role: Decomposers (recycle nutrients), cause diseases, used in fermentation.

Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.q: What is a food chain? Give an example of a food chain with four organisms.
Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.solution: A food chain is a linear sequence of organisms where energy flows from one organism to the next through feeding relationships. Example: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake. Each organism is a link in the chain, and energy is transferred from the producer (plant) through consumers at different levels.

Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.q: Define trophic levels and explain the difference between producers and consumers.
Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.solution: Trophic levels are the different feeding positions in a food chain. Producers (plants) are at the first trophic level and convert sunlight into chemical energy. Consumers feed on other organisms: primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers, secondary consumers (carnivores) eat primary consumers, and tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers.
