Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.q: What is an energy pyramid? Why does energy decrease at each trophic level?
Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.solution: An energy pyramid is a graphical representation showing energy distribution across trophic levels. Energy decreases at each level because: (1) only 10% of energy from one level passes to the next, (2) the rest is lost as heat during respiration, movement, and metabolic activities, (3) some energy is not consumed. This is why ecosystems can support fewer organisms at higher trophic levels.

Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.q: Explain the role of decomposers in the energy flow of an ecosystem.
Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.solution: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organic matter from all trophic levels, releasing nutrients back into the soil for plants to use. They obtain energy from dead organisms and return inorganic nutrients to the ecosystem, completing the nutrient cycle and maintaining ecosystem balance.

Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.q: What percentage of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next? Why is it not 100%?
Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.solution: Only about 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next. The remaining 90% is lost because: (1) much energy is used by organisms for respiration and body maintenance, (2) some energy is lost as heat, (3) not all parts of an organism are consumed, and (4) energy is needed for growth and reproduction, making ecosystems pyramidal in structure.

Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.q: Give examples of primary consumers, secondary consumers, and tertiary consumers in a grassland ecosystem.
Maharashtra::9::Science::energy-flow-in-.solution: In a grassland ecosystem: Primary consumers (herbivores) include grasshoppers, rabbits, and deer that feed on grasses. Secondary consumers (carnivores) include snakes and eagles that feed on herbivores. Tertiary consumers include hawks and large predators that feed on secondary consumers. The sun provides initial energy converted by grass (producer).

Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.q: Define microbes and name four types of microorganisms.
Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.solution: Microbes are microscopic organisms invisible to the naked eye. Four main types are: (1) Bacteria - unicellular, prokaryotic organisms, (2) Viruses - non-living infectious agents, (3) Fungi - eukaryotic organisms like yeasts and molds, (4) Protozoa - single-celled eukaryotes. Microbes are found everywhere in nature.

Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.q: List five useful microbes and their applications in daily life or industry.
Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.solution: Useful microbes include: (1) Lactobacillus in yogurt production improving digestion, (2) Yeast in bread and beer fermentation, (3) Rhizobium bacteria fixing nitrogen in soil for plant growth, (4) Streptomyces producing antibiotics like streptomycin, (5) Aspergillus in soy sauce and cheese production. These microbes benefit human health and industry.

Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.q: Name five diseases caused by harmful microbes and identify the causative agent for each.
Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.solution: Five harmful microbe diseases: (1) Tuberculosis - caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (bacteria), (2) Measles - caused by measles virus, (3) Malaria - caused by Plasmodium protozoan, (4) Cholera - caused by Vibrio cholerae bacteria, (5) Candidiasis - caused by Candida fungus. These pathogens cause serious health problems.

Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.q: How do beneficial bacteria in the human gut help our digestion and health?
Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.solution: Beneficial gut bacteria (like E. coli and Lactobacillus) help by: (1) producing vitamin K and B vitamins essential for health, (2) breaking down complex carbohydrates we cannot digest alone, (3) producing short-chain fatty acids that nourish intestinal cells, (4) preventing harmful bacteria from establishing infection, (5) strengthening our immune system. A balanced gut microbiome is crucial for health.

Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.q: Explain how microbes are used in wastewater treatment and bioremediation.
Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.solution: Microbes are used in wastewater treatment through aerobic and anaerobic processes where bacteria break down organic matter and nutrients, purifying water for safe discharge or reuse. In bioremediation, specific bacteria and fungi degrade pollutants, heavy metals, and toxic substances from contaminated soil and water. This natural process is cost-effective and environmentally friendly.

Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.q: What are pathogenic microbes and how do they cause disease? Mention three disease prevention methods.
Maharashtra::9::Science::useful-and-harm.solution: Pathogenic microbes are disease-causing organisms that invade the body, multiply, and damage cells through toxins or direct destruction. Three prevention methods: (1) Vaccination - building immunity before infection, (2) Hygiene and sanitation - preventing microbial entry and transmission, (3) Antibiotics and antimicrobials - killing or inhibiting harmful microbes. Maintaining cleanliness reduces disease spread.

Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.q: Define biodiversity and explain its importance for ecosystem stability and human survival.
Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.solution: Biodiversity refers to the variety of all living organisms (plants, animals, microbes) in an ecosystem. Its importance: (1) ensures ecosystem stability and resilience, (2) provides food, medicines, and resources for humans, (3) maintains nutrient cycles and oxygen production, (4) offers genetic diversity for adaptation to environmental changes, (5) provides economic and cultural benefits. Losing biodiversity threatens all life.

Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.q: List five major causes of environmental pollution and their harmful effects on living organisms.
Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.solution: Five pollution types: (1) Air pollution from vehicle emissions causes respiratory diseases and acid rain, (2) Water pollution from industrial waste causes fish death and contaminated drinking water, (3) Soil pollution from pesticides reduces fertility and harms organisms, (4) Noise pollution causes hearing loss and stress, (5) Plastic pollution persists for centuries, harming marine life and entering food chains. All damage ecosystems and human health.

Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.q: What is conservation of forests? Name three benefits of forest conservation.
Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.solution: Forest conservation is the protection and sustainable management of forests to maintain their ecological value. Three benefits: (1) Carbon sequestration reduces greenhouse gases and slows climate change, (2) Prevents soil erosion and maintains water cycles, (3) Preserves biodiversity and habitat for countless species, and protects tribal communities dependent on forests. Forests are essential for atmospheric oxygen and climate regulation.

Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.q: Explain the concept of sustainable development and how it relates to environmental management.
Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.solution: Sustainable development is meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs. It relates to environmental management by: (1) using renewable resources responsibly, (2) reducing waste and pollution, (3) protecting ecosystems and biodiversity, (4) promoting clean energy and sustainable agriculture, (5) balancing economic growth with environmental protection. This ensures long-term environmental and human survival.

Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.q: What is the ozone layer and why is its protection important? Name one cause of ozone depletion.
Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.solution: The ozone layer is a region in the stratosphere containing ozone gas that blocks harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from reaching Earth. Its protection is important because UV radiation causes skin cancer, eye damage, and immune suppression in humans, and damages crops and marine life. CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) from refrigerants and aerosols are a major cause of ozone depletion through photochemical reactions.

Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.q: Describe four methods of waste management and their environmental benefits.
Maharashtra::9::Science::environmental-m.solution: Four waste management methods: (1) Recycling converts waste into new products, reducing landfill burden and saving resources, (2) Composting decomposes organic waste into nutrient-rich soil amendment for agriculture, (3) Incineration reduces waste volume but requires emission controls, (4) Landfilling is controlled disposal but requires proper site selection. Proper waste management prevents pollution and conserves natural resources.

Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.q: What is Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and list five applications of ICT in science education.
Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.solution: ICT refers to technology used to process, transmit, and display information through computers and networks. Five ICT applications in science: (1) Virtual labs for safe experimentation and visualization, (2) Online simulations of complex phenomena like molecular interactions, (3) Digital microscopes for detailed observation and image capture, (4) Educational software for interactive learning and practice, (5) Video conferencing for distance learning and collaboration. ICT enhances science understanding.

Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.q: Explain the components of a basic computer system and their functions.
Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.solution: A basic computer has: (1) Input devices (keyboard, mouse) for user data entry, (2) CPU and RAM for processing and temporary storage of information, (3) Hard drive for permanent data storage, (4) Output devices (monitor, printer) for displaying results, (5) Power supply for electrical power. These components work together to receive input, process it, and produce output.

Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.q: What is the internet and how does it facilitate scientific research and learning?
Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.solution: The internet is a global network of interconnected computers sharing information via data protocols. It facilitates science research by: (1) providing instant access to scientific databases and journals, (2) enabling global collaboration between scientists, (3) allowing real-time data sharing and peer review, (4) offering online courses and tutorials for learning, (5) hosting scientific forums for discussion and problem-solving. The internet democratizes access to knowledge.

Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.q: Define software and explain the difference between system software and application software.
Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.solution: Software is a set of instructions that directs computer hardware to perform tasks. System software (like Windows, Linux) manages hardware resources and provides a platform for applications. Application software (like MS Word, MATLAB, educational programs) performs specific user tasks like document creation, data analysis, or learning simulations. Together they enable computers to function effectively.

Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.q: How can ICT tools be used to monitor environmental conditions in real-time?
Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.solution: ICT tools monitor environment through: (1) Sensor networks measuring temperature, humidity, air quality, and water parameters continuously, (2) Data loggers recording measurements over time, (3) Satellites for weather prediction and ecosystem monitoring, (4) Software analyzing large datasets to identify trends and anomalies, (5) Online dashboards displaying real-time environmental data to scientists and public. This enables rapid detection of environmental problems and informed decision-making.

Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.q: Discuss the importance of cybersecurity and data privacy in online learning and scientific research.
Maharashtra::9::Science::information-com.solution: Cybersecurity and data privacy are crucial for: (1) Protecting personal information and preventing identity theft in online learning platforms, (2) Securing sensitive research data from unauthorized access and theft, (3) Ensuring authenticity and integrity of scientific results, (4) Building trust in e-learning and research systems, (5) Complying with legal and ethical standards. Strong passwords, encryption, and secure connections are essential for safe online activities.

Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.q: State the two laws of reflection of light and explain each with an example.
Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.solution: Law 1: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal). Law 2: The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane. Example: When light hits a mirror at 30° from normal, it reflects at 30° on the other side. These laws apply to all reflective surfaces and enable accurate prediction of light paths.

Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.q: Differentiate between regular reflection and diffuse reflection. Where do they occur in daily life?
Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.solution: Regular reflection occurs on smooth, polished surfaces like mirrors and still water, where parallel rays reflect parallel, forming clear images. Diffuse reflection occurs on rough surfaces like paper and walls, where rays scatter in different directions due to surface irregularities, preventing clear image formation. Regular reflection is used in mirrors and telescopes; diffuse reflection allows us to see non-luminous objects from all angles.

Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.q: Define a concave mirror and explain how it forms real, virtual, magnified, and diminished images based on object position.
Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.solution: A concave mirror has an inward-curved reflecting surface that converges light rays. Image types depend on object position: (1) Beyond center - real, inverted, diminished, (2) At center - real, inverted, same size, (3) Between center and focus - real, inverted, magnified, (4) At focus - no image forms, (5) Between focus and mirror - virtual, erect, magnified. Concave mirrors focus light for applications like solar furnaces and flashlights.

Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.q: Describe the characteristics of images formed by a convex mirror and explain their practical applications.
Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.solution: A convex mirror has an outward-curved surface that diverges light rays. Images formed are: virtual (behind mirror), erect, diminished, and formed between pole and focus regardless of object position. Practical applications: (1) Vehicle side mirrors for wide field of view, (2) Security mirrors in shops and corners, (3) Safety reflectors on roads. Convex mirrors reduce blind spots and provide safety advantages.

Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.q: What is the focal length of a mirror? How does it relate to the radius of curvature?
Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.solution: Focal length (f) is the distance from the mirror's pole to the focal point where parallel rays converge (concave) or diverge from (convex). Radius of curvature (R) is the distance from the pole to the center of the circular surface. They relate by: f = R/2. For a concave mirror, f is positive; for a convex mirror, f is negative. This relationship helps calculate image positions using the mirror equation.

Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.q: Explain the mirror equation and solve a numerical example: An object 5 cm tall is placed 30 cm from a concave mirror with focal length 10 cm. Find image distance and magnification.
Maharashtra::9::Science::reflection-of-l.solution: Mirror equation: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, where u is object distance and v is image distance. Given: h = 5 cm, u = 30 cm, f = 10 cm. Calculation: 1/10 = 1/30 + 1/v, so 1/v = 1/10 - 1/30 = 2/30, v = 15 cm. Magnification m = -v/u = -15/30 = -0.5. Image is 15 cm from mirror, real, inverted, and half the object size.

Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.q: Define sound and explain how sound is produced. What type of wave is sound?
Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.solution: Sound is a form of energy that reaches our ears through vibrations and creates the sensation of hearing. Sound is produced when objects vibrate, creating oscillations that travel through a medium (air, water, solid) as longitudinal waves where particles vibrate parallel to wave direction. Sound requires a medium - it cannot travel through vacuum. Sound waves have specific frequency, wavelength, and amplitude properties.

Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.q: Describe the properties of sound: frequency, wavelength, amplitude, and speed. How are they related?
Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.solution: Sound properties: (1) Frequency (Hz) - number of vibrations per second, determines pitch (higher frequency = higher pitch), (2) Wavelength - distance between consecutive compressions or rarefactions, (3) Amplitude - maximum displacement from equilibrium, determines loudness, (4) Speed - about 340 m/s in air at 25°C, depends on medium. Relationship: Speed = Frequency × Wavelength.

Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.q: What is the Doppler effect? Give a real-life example and explain how frequency changes.
Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.solution: The Doppler effect is the apparent change in frequency when a sound source moves relative to an observer. Example: An ambulance siren sounds higher-pitched when approaching and lower when receding. When source approaches observer, sound waves compress (shorter wavelength), increasing frequency and pitch. When receding, waves stretch, decreasing frequency and pitch. This occurs with any moving sound source.

Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.q: Explain the phenomenon of echo and reverberation. How are they different?
Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.solution: Echo occurs when sound reflects from a distant surface and reaches the observer as a distinct, delayed sound after the original sound ends. The delay must be >0.1 seconds for human hearing. Reverberation occurs when sound reflects from nearby surfaces with overlapping echoes creating a continuous sound even after the source stops. Echo is a single distinct reflection; reverberation is multiple rapid reflections creating a trailing effect in rooms and auditoriums.

Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.q: What is the speed of sound in different media? Explain why it varies with the medium.
Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.solution: Speed of sound: In air (20°C) = 340 m/s, in water = 1500 m/s, in steel = 5000 m/s. Speed increases with medium density and elasticity because: (1) Denser, more elastic materials allow faster particle vibration transmission, (2) Stronger molecular bonds enable quicker momentum transfer, (3) Looser gases like air have slower propagation. Temperature also affects speed - higher temperature increases particle motion, increasing sound speed.

Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.q: Define sound intensity and loudness. How is sound intensity measured? What is the decibel scale?
Maharashtra::9::Science::study-of-sound.solution: Sound intensity is the power transmitted per unit area (measured in watts/m²), an objective physical quantity. Loudness is the subjective perception of sound in human ears. Intensity is measured using microphones and sound level meters. The decibel (dB) scale compares sound intensity to reference intensity (10^-12 W/m²): dB = 10 log(I/I₀). Normal conversation is 60 dB, loud music 100 dB, pain threshold 130 dB. The logarithmic scale reflects how human hearing works.

Maharashtra::9::Science::carbon-an-impor.q: What is carbon? Name any three allotropes of carbon.
Maharashtra::9::Science::carbon-an-impor.solution: Carbon is a non-metallic element with atomic number 6. Its three allotropes are: 1) Diamond - hardest form, used in cutting tools and jewelry. 2) Graphite - soft, conducts electricity, used in pencils. 3) Coal - porous, used as fuel and in filters.

Maharashtra::9::Science::carbon-an-impor.q: Explain covalent bonding in carbon compounds with an example.
Maharashtra::9::Science::carbon-an-impor.solution: Carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons with other atoms. In methane (CH4), carbon shares one electron with each of four hydrogen atoms, forming four C-H covalent bonds. This allows carbon to form stable molecules with various elements.

Tetravalency means carbon has a valency of 4, allowing it to form four covalent bonds with other atoms. This property enables carbon to form diverse organic compounds including hydrocarbons, alcohols, and carboxylic acids.

Maharashtra::9::Science::carbon-an-impor.q: Distinguish between diamond and graphite based on their structure and properties.
Maharashtra::9::Science::carbon-an-impor.solution: Diamond: Each carbon atom is bonded to four other carbons in a tetrahedral arrangement, making it extremely hard and transparent. Graphite: Carbon atoms form layers with weak van der Waals forces between them, making it soft, slippery, and electrically conductive.

Maharashtra::9::Science::carbon-an-impor.q: What is an organic compound? Give two examples.
Maharashtra::9::Science::carbon-an-impor.solution: Organic compounds contain carbon and hydrogen, often with oxygen and nitrogen. They are produced by living organisms or synthesized in labs. Examples: Methane (CH4) - simplest hydrocarbon found in natural gas. Glucose (C6H12O6) - sugar produced during photosynthesis.

Maharashtra::9::Science::carbon-an-impor.q: Explain why carbon forms so many compounds.
Maharashtra::9::Science::carbon-an-impor.solution: Carbon forms numerous compounds because of its tetravalency, small atomic size, and ability to form strong covalent bonds. It can bond with itself to form chains (catenation) and with various other elements, creating millions of diverse organic molecules.

Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.q: What is a soap? How is soap prepared?
Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.solution: Soap is a salt of a higher fatty acid, used for cleaning. Preparation: When an ester (fat or oil) reacts with sodium hydroxide solution, it undergoes saponification, producing glycerol and soap. This reaction is called ester hydrolysis or saponification reaction.

Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.q: How does soap cleanse dirt and oil?
Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.solution: Soap has two ends: hydrophobic tail (water-repelling) attaches to oil/dirt, and hydrophilic head (water-attracting) dissolves in water. This forms micelles where oil is trapped inside, allowing dirt to mix with water and be washed away during rinsing.

Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.q: What is the composition and uses of glass?
Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.solution: Glass is made from silica sand (SiO2), soda ash (Na2CO3), and limestone (CaCO3) heated to high temperature. Uses: window panes for buildings, bottles for storage, laboratory apparatus, optical lenses, and decorative items.

Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.q: Explain the manufacturing of cement and its uses.
Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.solution: Cement is made by heating limestone and clay at very high temperatures in a kiln, then grinding with gypsum. Uses: Concrete and mortar for construction, binding material in buildings, roads, bridges, and dams. It hardens when mixed with water.

Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.q: What are fertilisers? Name two types and their functions.
Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.solution: Fertilisers are substances added to soil to increase plant growth and crop yield. Types: Nitrogenous fertilisers (urea, ammonium nitrate) provide nitrogen for leaf growth. Phosphatic fertilisers (superphosphate) promote root development and flowering.

Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.q: What is ceramic? Give three examples of ceramic products.
Maharashtra::9::Science::substances-in-c.solution: Ceramic is made from clay minerals heated to high temperature, producing hard, brittle, heat-resistant material. Examples: Pottery and earthenware for vessels, porcelain for tableware and decorative items, tiles for floors and walls.

Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.q: Define nutrition. What are the two types of nutrition in organisms?
Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.solution: Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain and utilize food for growth, energy, and maintenance. Two types: 1) Autotrophic nutrition - organisms like plants manufacture their own food using light energy. 2) Heterotrophic nutrition - organisms like animals obtain food from other organisms.

Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.q: Explain the process of photosynthesis in plants.
Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.solution: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to produce glucose and oxygen. Equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2. This provides food for the plant and releases oxygen essential for respiration.

Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.q: What is respiration? Distinguish between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.solution: Respiration is the process of breaking down glucose to release energy. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and occurs in mitochondria, yielding maximum energy (38 ATP). Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen in cytoplasm, producing less energy and lactate or ethanol as byproducts.

Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.q: Describe the structure and function of a mitochondrion.
Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.solution: Mitochondrion has a double membrane envelope with inner folds called cristae. It contains enzymes for cellular respiration. Function: Powerhouse of the cell - breaks down glucose to produce ATP, the main energy currency for all cellular activities.

Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.q: What is cell division? Name two types of cell division.
Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.solution: Cell division is the process by which a cell reproduces to form new cells. Two types: 1) Mitosis - produces two identical daughter cells for growth and repair. 2) Meiosis - produces four non-identical gametes with half the chromosomes for sexual reproduction.

Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.q: Briefly explain the phases of mitosis.
Maharashtra::9::Science::life-processes-.solution: Mitosis has four phases: 1) Prophase - chromosomes condense, spindle forms. 2) Metaphase - chromosomes align at cell center. 3) Anaphase - sister chromatids separate and move apart. 4) Telophase - nuclear envelopes reform, cytokinesis completes division.

Maharashtra::9::Science::heredity-and-va.q: Define heredity and variation. Why is variation important?
Maharashtra::9::Science::heredity-and-va.solution: Heredity is the transmission of traits from parents to offspring through genes. Variation is differences in traits among organisms in a population. Variation is important for evolution, adaptation, and survival - populations with variation can adapt to environmental changes better.

Maharashtra::9::Science::heredity-and-va.q: What is a chromosome? How many chromosomes are found in human cells?
Maharashtra::9::Science::heredity-and-va.solution: A chromosome is a structure in the cell nucleus containing DNA and proteins. It carries genes responsible for hereditary traits. Human cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), with 44 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males).

Mendel's law of segregation states that during gamete formation, paired alleles separate so that each gamete receives only one allele for a trait. During fertilization, alleles from parents combine, restoring the pair in offspring. This explains how traits skip generations.

Maharashtra::9::Science::heredity-and-va.q: What is a gene? What is the relationship between genes and traits?
Maharashtra::9::Science::heredity-and-va.solution: A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a specific protein and determines a particular trait. Each gene occupies a specific position (locus) on a chromosome. Traits result from the expression of genes - different alleles of a gene produce different variations of a trait.

Maharashtra::9::Science::heredity-and-va.q: Define dominant and recessive traits with an example.
Maharashtra::9::Science::heredity-and-va.solution: Dominant trait is expressed when at least one dominant allele is present. Recessive trait is expressed only when two recessive alleles are present. Example: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over short (t). TT and Tt are tall; tt is short.

Maharashtra::9::Science::heredity-and-va.q: What is DNA? State its full form and main function.
Maharashtra::9::Science::heredity-and-va.solution: DNA is deoxyribonucleic acid, the molecule carrying genetic information in all living organisms. It consists of four bases (A, T, G, C) arranged in a double helix structure. Main function: Stores and transmits hereditary information from generation to generation.

Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.q: Define biotechnology. What are its main fields of application?
Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.solution: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their products to solve practical problems and produce useful substances. Main fields: Agricultural biotechnology (improved crops), Medical biotechnology (vaccines, medicines), Industrial biotechnology (fermentation), Environmental biotechnology (biofuels, waste treatment).

Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.q: What is genetic engineering? Give one example of a genetically modified organism.
Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.solution: Genetic engineering is the process of introducing foreign DNA into an organism to impart new traits. Example: Bt cotton has a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis inserted into its genome, making it resistant to cotton pests, reducing pesticide use.

Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.q: Explain the application of biotechnology in medicine.
Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.solution: Biotechnology produces insulin for diabetes treatment using genetically engineered bacteria. It develops vaccines for diseases like polio and COVID-19. Gene therapy treats genetic disorders by replacing defective genes. Monoclonal antibodies help diagnose and treat cancer and autoimmune diseases.

Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.q: What is fermentation? Name one industrial application.
Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.solution: Fermentation is an anaerobic process where microorganisms break down glucose to produce useful products without oxygen. Industrial application: Production of yogurt - lactic acid bacteria ferment milk lactose, producing lactic acid that curdles milk, creating yogurt with increased shelf life.

Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.q: How is biotechnology used in agriculture?
Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.solution: Biotechnology creates disease-resistant varieties and increased-yield crops through selective breeding and genetic modification. Examples: Golden rice enriched with vitamin A, drought-resistant wheat varieties, pest-resistant crops. This improves food security and reduces crop losses.

Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.q: What are the ethical concerns related to biotechnology?
Maharashtra::9::Science::introduction-to.solution: Ethical concerns include: Unknown long-term effects of GMOs on human health and ecosystems. Intellectual property issues and patent laws restricting farmer access to seeds. Environmental risks of gene flow to wild plants. Safety regulations and labeling requirements for genetically modified foods.

Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.q: What is a telescope? What are the two main types of telescopes?
Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.solution: A telescope is an optical instrument used to observe distant objects in space by magnifying their size and brightness. Two types: 1) Refracting telescope - uses a convex lens to focus light. 2) Reflecting telescope - uses a concave mirror to focus light and is preferred for large telescopes.

Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.q: Explain how a refracting telescope works.
Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.solution: A refracting telescope has two convex lenses: the objective lens (larger, at one end) focuses light from a distant object to form a real image. The eyepiece lens (smaller, at the other end) acts as a magnifying glass, creating a magnified virtual image visible to the observer.

Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.q: What is a reflecting telescope? What are its advantages over refracting telescopes?
Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.solution: A reflecting telescope uses a large concave primary mirror to collect and focus light, and a small plane mirror directs the image to the eyepiece. Advantages: Can be made much larger without optical defects, produces sharper images, doesn't suffer from chromatic aberration, and is less expensive.

Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.q: Define the terms: light year and astronomical unit.
Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.solution: Light year is the distance light travels in one year in vacuum, approximately 9.46 trillion km. Used to measure vast distances between stars and galaxies. Astronomical unit (AU) is the average distance between Earth and Sun, approximately 150 million km, used for distances within the solar system.

Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.q: Name the eight planets in our solar system in order from the Sun.
Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.solution: The eight planets in order are: 1) Mercury - smallest, closest to Sun. 2) Venus - hottest planet. 3) Earth - our home. 4) Mars - red planet. 5) Jupiter - largest planet. 6) Saturn - has prominent rings. 7) Uranus - rotates on its side. 8) Neptune - farthest from Sun.

Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.q: What is a constellation? Name two constellations visible from India.
Maharashtra::9::Science::observing-space.solution: A constellation is a recognizable pattern of stars as seen from Earth, named after mythological figures or objects. Two constellations visible from India: 1) Orion (Hunter) - visible in winter, contains bright star Betelgeuse. 2) Ursa Major (Big Bear) - visible year-round, contains the Big Dipper.

TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.q: Define focal length of a spherical mirror.
TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.solution:
Focal length (f) is the distance between the pole (P) of the mirror and its focal point (F).
It is half the radius of curvature: f = R/2
Where R is the radius of curvature of the mirror.

TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.q: A concave mirror has radius of curvature 20 cm. Find its focal length.
TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.solution:
Step 1: Given R = 20 cm
Step 2: Use formula f = R/2
Step 3: f = 20/2 = 10 cm
Focal length = 10 cm

TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.q: An object 4 cm tall is placed 30 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find image distance and magnification.
TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.solution:
Step 1: Given h = 4 cm, u = 30 cm, f = 10 cm
Step 2: Use mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u
Step 3: 1/10 = 1/v + 1/30 → 1/v = 1/10 - 1/30 = 2/30 = 1/15
Step 4: v = 15 cm (real image)
Step 5: Magnification m = -v/u = -15/30 = -0.5
Image distance = 15 cm, magnification = -0.5 (inverted, reduced)

TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.q: Why does a concave mirror form a real, inverted, diminished image when object is beyond C?
TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.solution:
When object is beyond center of curvature (C):
• Light rays converge after reflection
• Image forms between C and F on the same side
• Image is real (can be projected on screen), inverted, and smaller than object
• This follows from the principle that rays obey mirror formula and geometry

TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.q: What is the power of a concave mirror with focal length 25 cm?
TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.solution:
Step 1: Given f = 25 cm = 0.25 m
Step 2: Power P = 1/f (in diopters, when f in meters)
Step 3: P = 1/0.25 = +4 diopters
Power = +4 D (positive because it's concave/converging)

TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.q: Define magnification and state its sign convention for mirrors.
TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.solution:
Magnification (m) = height of image / height of object = -v/u
Sign convention: m is positive when image is erect (virtual), negative when inverted (real)
For mirrors: Real images have negative m, virtual images have positive m

TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.q: A concave mirror is used in a shaving mirror. Why?
TS::10::Science::reflection-of-light-at-.solution:
A concave mirror forms an erect, magnified virtual image when object is between pole and focus.
This magnified virtual image helps in proper shaving and grooming.
The concave shape concentrates light and provides clear, enlarged view of the face.

TS::10::Science::chemical-equations.q: What is a chemical equation? Explain with an example.
TS::10::Science::chemical-equations.solution:
A chemical equation is a symbolic representation of a chemical reaction using formulas and symbols.
Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
Left side (reactants) = elements/compounds that react
Right side (products) = new substances formed
Numbers (coefficients) show molar ratios to balance atoms

TS::10::Science::chemical-equations.q: Balance the equation: Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃
TS::10::Science::chemical-equations.solution:
Step 1: Count atoms on each side
Reactants: Fe=1, O=2 | Products: Fe=2, O=3
Step 2: Balance Fe: multiply Fe by 4 → 4Fe
Step 3: Balance O: need 6 oxygen atoms, multiply O₂ by 3 → 3O₂
Step 4: Balanced equation: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃
Verify: Fe=4 both sides, O=6 both sides ✓

TS::10::Science::chemical-equations.q: Define decomposition reaction with two examples.
TS::10::Science::chemical-equations.solution:
Decomposition reaction: A single compound breaks into two or more simpler substances.
Example 1: 2PbO → 2Pb + O₂ (lead oxide decomposes)
Example 2: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (hydrogen peroxide decomposes)
These are reverse of combination reactions

TS::10::Science::chemical-equations.q: What is a displacement reaction? Give one example.
TS::10::Science::chemical-equations.solution:
Displacement reaction: An element displaces another element from its compound.
Example: Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag
Here copper displaces silver from silver nitrate.
Reactivity order must be followed: more reactive element displaces less reactive one

Step 1: Count atoms
Left: C=1, O=2 | Right: C=1, O=2
Step 2: Already balanced (no coefficients needed)
Balanced equation: C + O₂ → CO₂
Verify: C=1, O=2 on both sides ✓

TS::10::Science::chemical-equations.q: What is a double displacement reaction? Name one example.
TS::10::Science::chemical-equations.solution:
Double displacement reaction: Two compounds exchange their ions to form two new compounds.
Example: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃
Here Ag⁺ and Na⁺ exchange places with NO₃⁻ and Cl⁻
Usually involves precipitation (↓), gas evolution (↑), or water formation

Step 1: Count atoms
Left: Ca=1, O=2, H=3, Cl=1 | Right: Ca=1, Cl=2, H=2, O=1
Step 2: Balance Cl by multiplying HCl by 2: 2HCl
Step 3: Balance H and O by multiplying H₂O by 2: 2H₂O
Step 4: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O
Verify: Ca=1, O=2, H=4, Cl=2 both sides ✓

TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.q: Define acid and base according to Arrhenius theory.
TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.solution:
Acid: A substance that produces H⁺ ions (or H₃O⁺) when dissolved in water.
Example: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻
Base: A substance that produces OH⁻ ions when dissolved in water.
Example: NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻
Arrhenius definitions apply only in aqueous solutions

TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.q: What is pH? Write pH values for acidic, neutral, and basic solutions.
TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.solution:
pH = -log₁₀[H⁺ concentration]
It measures the acidity or alkalinity of a solution.
Acidic solution: pH < 7 (example: pH = 2 for HCl)
Neutral solution: pH = 7 (pure water)
Basic/Alkaline solution: pH > 7 (example: pH = 10 for NaOH)
Range: 0-14 (pH scale)

TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.q: Distinguish between strong and weak acids with examples.
TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.solution:
Strong acid: Completely ionizes in water, produces many H⁺ ions.
Examples: HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃
Weak acid: Partially ionizes in water, produces few H⁺ ions.
Examples: CH₃COOH (acetic acid), H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid)
Strong acids have lower pH than weak acids of same concentration

TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.q: What happens when an acid reacts with a base? Name the products.
TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.solution:
Acid + Base → Salt + Water (Neutralization reaction)
Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O
Here: HCl is acid, NaOH is base
Products: NaCl is salt (neutral), H₂O is water
The H⁺ from acid combines with OH⁻ from base to form water

TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.q: Define salt. Give three examples of salts.
TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.solution:
Salt: An ionic compound formed by neutralization of an acid with a base.
Composition: Positive ions (cations) from base + negative ions (anions) from acid.
Examples:
1. NaCl (sodium chloride) from HCl + NaOH
2. CuSO₄ (copper sulfate) from H₂SO₄ + Cu(OH)₂
3. KNO₃ (potassium nitrate) from HNO₃ + KOH

TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.q: What is the action of universal indicator on acids, bases, and neutral solutions?
TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.solution:
Universal indicator is a mixture of dyes that shows different colors at different pH values.
With acid (pH < 7): Red/orange color
With neutral solution (pH = 7): Green color
With base (pH > 7): Blue/violet color
The color change helps identify if solution is acidic, basic, or neutral

TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.q: Why is HCl a strong acid while CH₃COOH is a weak acid?
TS::10::Science::acids-bases-and-salts.solution:
HCl: Completely ionizes: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ (strong acid)
CH₃COOH: Partially ionizes: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (weak acid, equilibrium symbol)
HCl produces more H⁺ ions per molecule, making it strongly acidic.
CH₃COOH produces fewer H⁺ ions, remaining partially unionized in solution

TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.q: Define refraction of light. State Snell's law.
TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.solution:
Refraction: Bending of light when it passes from one medium to another of different optical density.
Snell's Law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
Where n = refractive index, θ = angle of incidence/refraction
Light bends toward normal when entering denser medium, away from normal when entering rarer medium

TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.q: What is a lens? Distinguish between convex and concave lenses.
TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.solution:
Lens: A transparent optical device with curved surfaces for refraction of light.
Convex lens (converging): Thicker at center, thinner at edges. Converges parallel rays to focal point. Forms real/virtual images.
Concave lens (diverging): Thinner at center, thicker at edges. Diverges parallel rays. Forms only virtual, erect, diminished images.
Both lenses obey lens formula and follow sign convention

TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.q: A convex lens has focal length 20 cm. Find image position and nature when object is at 40 cm.
TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.solution:
Step 1: Given f = 20 cm, u = 40 cm (object distance)
Step 2: Use lens formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u
Step 3: 1/20 = 1/v + 1/40 → 1/v = 1/20 - 1/40 = 1/40
Step 4: v = 40 cm (image distance)
Step 5: Magnification m = v/u = 40/40 = 1
Image is at 40 cm, real, inverted, same size as object (magnification = 1)

TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.q: Define focal length and power of a lens.
TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.solution:
Focal length (f): Distance between optical center and focal point of a lens.
For convex lens, f is positive; for concave lens, f is negative.
Power (P): Reciprocal of focal length in meters.
P = 1/f (in diopters, D)
Example: f = 20 cm = 0.2 m, P = 1/0.2 = +5 D (convex lens)

TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.q: A concave lens has focal length 15 cm. Where will image form if object is at 30 cm?
TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.solution:
Step 1: Given f = -15 cm (concave, negative), u = 30 cm
Step 2: Use lens formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u
Step 3: 1/(-15) = 1/v + 1/30 → 1/v = -1/15 - 1/30 = -3/30 = -1/10
Step 4: v = -10 cm
Image forms at 10 cm on the same side as object, virtual, erect, diminished

TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.q: Why is a convex lens called a converging lens?
TS::10::Science::refraction-of-light-at-.solution:
A convex lens is thicker at center. When parallel rays pass through it, they refract (bend) toward the optical axis.
All rays converge at a single point called focal point (F).
This converging property helps in focusing light, magnifying objects, and forming real images.
Opposite to concave lens which diverges rays

Lens maker's formula: 1/f = (n-1)[1/R₁ - 1/R₂]
Where: f = focal length, n = refractive index of lens material, R₁ and R₂ = radii of curvature
Signs: R is positive for center of curvature on right side, negative on left side
Used to calculate focal length from lens geometry and material properties

TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.q: Draw and label the structure of human eye. Name three main parts.
TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.solution:
Human eye main parts:
1. Cornea: Transparent front layer, refracts light
2. Lens: Biconvex, adjustable focal length for accommodation
3. Retina: Light-sensitive layer at back, contains rods and cones, converts light to nerve signals
Other parts: Iris (controls pupil), ciliary muscles (adjust lens), optic nerve (sends signals to brain)

TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.q: What is accommodation of the eye? How does it work?
TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.solution:
Accommodation: Ability of eye to focus on objects at different distances.
Mechanism: Ciliary muscles contract to change the shape of lens.
For near objects: Ciliary muscles contract → lens becomes thicker → focal length decreases → image focuses on retina
For distant objects: Ciliary muscles relax → lens becomes thinner → focal length increases → image focuses on retina

TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.q: What is myopia? How is it corrected?
TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.solution:
Myopia (short-sightedness): Far objects appear blurred, near objects clear.
Cause: Eyeball too long OR cornea too curved → images form in front of retina
Correction: Concave lens (diverging) placed in front of eye.
Concave lens diverges rays before entering eye, shifting focus point back to retina.
Prescription uses negative power (e.g., -2.5 D)

Hypermetropia (long-sightedness): Near objects appear blurred, far objects clear.
Cause: Eyeball too short OR cornea too flat → images form behind retina
Correction: Convex lens (converging) placed in front of eye.
Convex lens converges rays before entering eye, shifting focus point forward to retina.
Prescription uses positive power (e.g., +2.5 D)

TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.q: What is dispersion of white light? Name the seven colors in order.
TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.solution:
Dispersion: Splitting of white light into constituent colors (spectrum) due to different refractive indices for different wavelengths.
Caused by: Prism or water droplets (rainbows)
Seven colors in order (VIBGYOR): Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red
Violet has smallest wavelength (bends most), Red has largest wavelength (bends least)

TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.q: Explain Rayleigh scattering. Why is the sky blue and sunset red?
TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.solution:
Rayleigh scattering: Scattering of light by particles much smaller than wavelength.
Intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴ (inversely proportional to fourth power of wavelength)
Blue light (shorter wavelength) scatters more than red light.
Sky appears blue: Blue light from sun scatters most in atmosphere during daytime.
Sunset appears red: At sunset, light travels long distance through atmosphere, blue scattered away, leaving red/orange light to reach observer

TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.q: What is astigmatism and how is it different from myopia?
TS::10::Science::human-eye-and-colourful.solution:
Astigmatism: Defect where eye cannot focus both horizontal and vertical lines simultaneously.
Cause: Cornea or lens has different curvatures in different planes (oval shape).
Difference from myopia: Myopia = unable to see far objects (whole image blurred). Astigmatism = unable to focus all lines equally (partial blur).
Correction: Cylindrical lens (corrects one plane) or toric lens

TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.q: State Dalton's atomic theory. Name two points.
TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.solution:
Dalton's Atomic Theory:
1. All matter is made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms.
2. Atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties; atoms of different elements differ.
3. Compounds form when atoms combine in fixed, simple whole-number ratios.
4. Chemical reactions involve rearrangement of atoms; atoms are neither created nor destroyed.

TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.q: Describe Rutherford's atomic model with a diagram description.
TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.solution:
Rutherford's Model:
• Atom has a dense, positively charged nucleus at center containing protons.
• Electrons orbit nucleus in circular paths (shells) at specific distances.
• Most of atom is empty space.
• Electrons experience centripetal force from nuclear charge.
Drawback: Model cannot explain electron stability (electrons should spiral into nucleus)

TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.q: What are the four quantum numbers? Explain principal quantum number (n).
TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.solution:
Four quantum numbers describe electron position in atom:
1. Principal quantum number (n): Determines energy level and size of orbit. n = 1,2,3,... (valence shell distance from nucleus)
2. Angular momentum quantum number (l): Determines subshell shape (s, p, d, f orbitals). l = 0,1,2,...(n-1)
3. Magnetic quantum number (m): Determines orientation of orbital in space.
4. Spin quantum number (s): Represents electron spin direction (+1/2 or -1/2)

TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.q: Define valency. How is valency related to electron configuration?
TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.solution:
Valency: Combining capacity of an element, equal to number of electrons lost/gained/shared to form bonds.
Relation to electron configuration: Elements combine to achieve stable configuration (usually 8 electrons in valence shell, or 2 for H/He).
Example: Cl has 7 valence electrons, needs 1 more → valency = 1 (gains 1 electron)
Na has 1 valence electron, loses it → valency = 1 (loses 1 electron)

TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.q: Compare Bohr's model with Rutherford's model. Name one difference.
TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.solution:
Rutherford's Model: Electrons orbit in circular paths with any radius. Does NOT explain stability of atoms.
Bohr's Model: Electrons orbit only in specific circular paths (quantized orbits) with definite energy. Explains hydrogen spectrum and atom stability.
Key difference: Bohr introduced concept of quantization (discrete energy levels), fixing electron orbits.
Bohr's model works for hydrogen but not for complex multi-electron atoms

TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.q: What is an isotope? Give an example.
TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.solution:
Isotope: Atoms of same element with same atomic number but different mass numbers (different number of neutrons).
Same number of protons → same element, same chemical properties
Different number of neutrons → different mass, different nuclear properties
Example: Carbon-12 (⁶C¹²) and Carbon-14 (⁶C¹⁴)
Both have 6 protons but different neutron numbers (6 and 8 respectively)

TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.q: How many electrons can be accommodated in the third shell (M shell)?
TS::10::Science::structure-of-atom.solution:
Using formula: Maximum electrons = 2n²
For third shell (M shell), n = 3
Maximum electrons = 2(3)² = 2(9) = 18 electrons
Electron distribution in M shell: 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰
However, in actual atoms, M shell can hold maximum 8 electrons as valence shell before N shell starts filling

TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.q: What is the modern periodic law? How does it differ from Mendeleev's law?
TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.solution:
Modern periodic law: Properties of elements repeat periodically when arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
Mendeleev's law: Properties repeat in order of increasing atomic mass (had gaps, some elements out of order).
Improvement: Moseley discovered atomic number is more fundamental than mass. Correcting by atomic number fixed anomalies (e.g., Ar before K, although heavier).
Modern law is universal and explains all known elements

TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.q: Define period and group in periodic table. Explain one trend.
TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.solution:
Period: Horizontal row in periodic table. Elements have same number of electron shells.
Group: Vertical column. Elements have same number of valence electrons, similar chemical properties.
Example trend - Atomic radius: Decreases from left to right across period (increasing nuclear charge with same shell)
Increases down a group (increasing number of shells).
Atom becomes larger down a group, smaller across period

TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.q: Explain electronegativity trend in the periodic table.
TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.solution:
Electronegativity: Ability of atom to attract electrons in a chemical bond.
Trend:
• Increases from left to right across period (more protons, stronger attraction)
• Decreases down a group (more shells, electrons farther from nucleus)
• Most electronegative: Fluorine (F) = 4.0
• Least electronegative: Francium (Fr) and Cesium (Cs) ≈ 0.7
Used to predict bond type: large difference → ionic, small difference → covalent

TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.q: What are representative elements? Name their block and group number.
TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.solution:
Representative elements: Elements in Groups 1, 2, 13-18 (s and p block).
Also called main group or normal elements.
Block: s-block (Groups 1, 2) and p-block (Groups 13-18)
Characteristic: Valence electrons in outermost s or p subshell.
Examples: Na (Group 1), Mg (Group 2), Al (Group 13), O (Group 16), F (Group 17)
These are most abundant and important elements in chemistry

TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.q: Arrange C, N, O, F in order of increasing atomic radius.
TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.solution:
Atomic radius decreases from left to right across period.
All four are in period 2.
Atomic number order: C(6) < N(7) < O(8) < F(9)
As atomic number increases, nuclear charge increases → electrons pulled closer → radius decreases
Order of increasing radius: F < O < N < C
Opposite order of increasing nuclear charge

TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.q: Classify elements into metals, non-metals, and metalloids. Give examples.
TS::10::Science::classification-of-eleme.solution:
Metals: Elements that lose electrons, conduct electricity, malleable, ductile, lustrous.
Examples: Fe, Cu, Al, Na, Ca (left and center of periodic table)
Non-metals: Elements that gain electrons, poor conductors, brittle, non-lustrous.
Examples: O, N, F, Cl, S, C (right side of periodic table, Group 13-18)
Metalloids: Elements with properties between metals and non-metals, semiconductors.
Examples: Si, Ge, As, Sb (staircase line between metals and non-metals)

Halogens have 7 valence electrons (Group 17).
They need only 1 more electron to achieve stable octet configuration (8 electrons).
Only one electron away from stability → very reactive, readily gain 1 electron to form X⁻ ions.
Example: F + e⁻ → F⁻ (most reactive because smallest, highest electronegativity)
Reactivity decreases down group: F > Cl > Br > I (atomic radius increases)

TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.q: Define chemical bond. Explain the difference between ionic and covalent bonds.
TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.solution:
Chemical bond: Force of attraction that holds atoms together in molecules or compounds.
Ionic bond: Formed by complete transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal. Results in electrostatic attraction between cations and anions. Example: NaCl (Na⁺ Cl⁻)
Covalent bond: Formed by sharing of electron pairs between non-metals. Electrons are shared equally (nonpolar) or unequally (polar). Example: Cl₂, H₂O
Ionic = transfer, Covalent = sharing

TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.q: What is an ionic bond? Explain formation of NaCl with electron dot structure.
TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.solution:
Ionic bond: Electrostatic force between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.
Formation of NaCl:
Na (11e⁻) → Na⁺ + 1e⁻ (loses 1 valence electron)
Cl (17e⁻) + 1e⁻ → Cl⁻ (gains 1 electron)
Na⁺ [Cl:⁻] (Cl with octet: 8 electrons, Na with empty M shell = 2 electrons in L shell)
Electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ forms ionic bond.
Result: Solid crystal lattice of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions

TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.q: Define covalent bond. Explain single, double, and triple bonds.
TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.solution:
Covalent bond: Chemical bond formed by sharing of electron pair(s) between non-metal atoms.
Single bond: Sharing of 1 electron pair (2 electrons).
Example: H—H (H₂) or C—C
Double bond: Sharing of 2 electron pairs (4 electrons).
Example: O=O (O₂) or C=O in CO₂
Triple bond: Sharing of 3 electron pairs (6 electrons).
Example: N≡N (N₂) or C≡C
Triple bond is strongest, single bond is weakest

TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.q: Draw Lewis dot structure for H₂O. Show electron distribution.
TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.solution:
Lewis structure of H₂O:
O has 6 valence electrons, each H has 1 valence electron.
Total = 6 + 1 + 1 = 8 electrons
Structure: H—O—H with 2 lone pairs on O
Electron distribution:
  ..O.. (4 dots for 2 lone pairs)
 H:O:H
O forms 2 single covalent bonds (2 pairs shared with H atoms)
O has 2 lone pairs (unshared electrons)
Each H achieves duet (2 electrons), O achieves octet (8 electrons)

TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.q: What is a polar covalent bond? Give an example.
TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.solution:
Polar covalent bond: Covalent bond in which electron pair is shared unequally between atoms.
Reason: Atoms have different electronegativities.
Electrons shift toward more electronegative atom → partial charges develop.
Example: H—Cl
Cl is more electronegative than H → electrons shift toward Cl
H becomes slightly positive (δ+), Cl becomes slightly negative (δ⁻)
Result: H^δ+ — Cl^δ⁻ (polar bond)
Other examples: H—O, H—N (all bonds to highly electronegative atoms)

TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.q: Distinguish between coordinate covalent bond and ordinary covalent bond.
TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.solution:
Ordinary covalent bond: Each atom contributes one electron to form shared pair.
Example: H—H (each H contributes 1 electron)
Coordinate covalent (dative) bond: Both electrons in shared pair come from one atom (donor), other atom accepts (acceptor). Still formed same way but origin is different.
Example: NH₄⁺ (ammonium ion) — N donates lone pair to H⁺
Once formed, coordinate bond is identical to ordinary covalent bond.
Symbol: → (shows direction from donor to acceptor) but often written as regular line

TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.q: Explain the formation of O₂ molecule using molecular orbital theory description.
TS::10::Science::chemical-bonding.solution:
O₂ formation:
Each O has 6 valence electrons, total = 12 electrons in O₂
Lewis structure shows double bond: O=O
Bond order = (bonding electrons - antibonding electrons)/2 = (8-4)/2 = 2
Double bond = 2 shared pairs (4 electrons)
Each O achieves octet configuration
O₂ is paramagnetic (has unpaired electrons in antibonding orbitals)
Bond strength is high due to double bond, explains why O₂ is stable molecule

TS::10::Science::electric-current.q: State Ohm's Law and explain what it means.
TS::10::Science::electric-current.solution:
Ohm's Law states: V = I × R, where V is potential difference (Volts), I is current (Amperes), and R is resistance (Ohms).

Meaning: At constant temperature, the potential difference across a conductor is directly proportional to the current flowing through it. The ratio V/I remains constant for a given conductor and is called its resistance.

Mathematically: R = V/I

TS::10::Science::electric-current.q: A wire has resistance 10 Ω. If a potential difference of 50 V is applied, find the current.
TS::10::Science::electric-current.solution:
Step 1: Given R = 10 Ω, V = 50 V
Step 2: Use Ohm's Law: V = I × R
Step 3: Rearrange: I = V/R = 50/10 = 5 A

Answer: Current = 5 Amperes

TS::10::Science::electric-current.q: Define electric resistance and list 3 factors affecting it.
TS::10::Science::electric-current.solution:
Resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of electric current through it. Unit: Ohm (Ω).

Three factors affecting resistance:
1. Length of conductor (L): Resistance ∝ L (longer wire = higher resistance)
2. Cross-sectional area (A): Resistance ∝ 1/A (thicker wire = lower resistance)
3. Nature of material (ρ): Different materials have different resistivity values

Formula: R = ρL/A

TS::10::Science::electric-current.q: Calculate the power consumed by a device if current 2 A flows through it at 220 V potential difference.
TS::10::Science::electric-current.solution:
Step 1: Given V = 220 V, I = 2 A
Step 2: Power formula: P = V × I
Step 3: P = 220 × 2 = 440 W

Answer: Power consumed = 440 Watts

Alternative: Using P = I²R or P = V²/R if R is known

TS::10::Science::electric-current.q: What is the difference between series and parallel circuits?
TS::10::Science::electric-current.solution:
Series Circuit:
• Components connected end-to-end in single path
• Same current flows through all components
• Total resistance: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃...
• If one breaks, entire circuit breaks

Parallel Circuit:
• Components connected with multiple paths
• Same voltage across all components
• Total resistance: 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃...
• If one breaks, others still work

TS::10::Science::electric-current.q: A bulb rated 60 W, 220 V is used for 5 hours. Calculate electrical energy consumed in kWh.
TS::10::Science::electric-current.solution:
Step 1: Given Power P = 60 W = 0.06 kW, Time t = 5 hours
Step 2: Energy formula: E = P × t
Step 3: E = 0.06 × 5 = 0.30 kWh

Answer: Energy consumed = 0.30 kWh or 0.3 units

Cost = 0.3 × Rate (where rate depends on local electricity charges)

TS::10::Science::electric-current.q: Explain the working principle of a circuit breaker and its importance.
TS::10::Science::electric-current.solution:
A circuit breaker is a safety device that automatically cuts off electric supply when current exceeds safe limits.

Working: When excessive current flows (due to overload or short circuit), the electromagnetic coil in the breaker generates strong magnetic field → trips the switch → breaks the circuit.

Importance:
1. Prevents fire caused by overheating of wires
2. Protects electrical appliances from damage
3. Saves lives from electric shock
4. Can be reset after tripping (unlike fuse which melts permanently)

TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.q: What is an electromagnet? Describe its construction and how it differs from a permanent magnet.
TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.solution:
An electromagnet is a magnet created by passing electric current through a coil of insulated wire wound around an iron core.

Construction: Insulated copper wire coiled around soft iron core + power source

Differences from permanent magnet:
1. Electromagnet requires electric current to be magnetic; permanent magnet has permanent magnetism
2. Strength of electromagnet can be controlled; permanent magnet has fixed strength
3. Electromagnet can be switched on/off; permanent magnet cannot
4. Electromagnet's polarity can be reversed; permanent magnet's polarity is fixed

TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.q: State and explain Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction.
TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.solution:
Faraday's Law: The induced EMF in a coil is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux through it.

Mathematically: e = -N(dΦ/dt)
where e = induced EMF, N = number of turns, dΦ/dt = rate of change of magnetic flux

Explanation: When magnetic field through a coil changes, an EMF (voltage) is induced. The negative sign indicates direction (Lenz's Law).

Practical example: Moving magnet near coil → magnetic field changes → EMF induced → current flows if circuit is closed

TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.q: Explain Fleming's Left Hand Rule and Fleming's Right Hand Rule with applications.
TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.solution:
Fleming's Left Hand Rule (Force on current-carrying wire in magnetic field):
Thumb = direction of force, Index finger = direction of magnetic field, Middle finger = direction of current
Application: Determines force direction in electric motors

Fleming's Right Hand Rule (Induced EMF/current in moving conductor):
Thumb = direction of motion, Index finger = direction of magnetic field, Middle finger = direction of induced current
Application: Determines induced current direction in generators

TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.q: Describe the construction and working of a simple electric motor.
TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.solution:
Construction:
• Rectangular coil of insulated copper wire
• Placed between two poles of a permanent magnet (N and S)
• Connected to a split-ring commutator
• Commutator rotates with coil, maintaining circuit contact via brushes

Working:
Step 1: Current enters coil via commutator
Step 2: Magnetic force acts on current-carrying coil (Fleming's Left Hand Rule)
Step 3: Coil rotates; commutator switches current direction at each half rotation
Step 4: Force always acts in same rotational direction → continuous rotation

Principle: Converts electrical energy to mechanical energy

TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.q: Explain the construction and working of a simple AC generator with a labeled diagram description.
TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.solution:
Construction:
• Rectangular coil rotating between magnetic poles (N-S)
• Slip rings attached to coil ends
• Brushes maintain circuit contact with slip rings
• External circuit/load connected via brushes

Working:
Step 1: Coil rotates in magnetic field (mechanical energy input)
Step 2: Magnetic flux through coil changes continuously
Step 3: Rate of flux change induces EMF (Faraday's Law)
Step 4: Induced EMF is sinusoidal: e = e₀sin(ωt)
Step 5: Current flows in external circuit

Principle: Converts mechanical energy to electrical energy

TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.q: What is the difference between AC and DC current? List 3 advantages of AC over DC.
TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.solution:
Difference:
DC (Direct Current): Flows in one direction; magnitude constant; produced by batteries, cells
AC (Alternating Current): Direction reverses periodically; magnitude varies sinusoidally; produced by generators

Advantages of AC over DC:
1. Easy transmission over long distances (voltage can be stepped up/down using transformers)
2. Stepping up voltage reduces current → reduces power loss in transmission (P_loss = I²R)
3. AC motors are simpler, cheaper, more efficient than DC motors
4. Easier to generate in bulk using generators

TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.q: Define magnetic field and explain what causes magnetism in a bar magnet at atomic level.
TS::10::Science::electromagnetism.solution:
Magnetic field is the region around a magnet where magnetic force can be experienced by another magnet or current-carrying conductor.

Cause of magnetism in bar magnet:
At atomic level, electrons possess spin and orbital motion → generate tiny magnetic moments
In permanent magnet materials (iron, cobalt, nickel): unpaired electrons' magnetic moments align in same direction → net magnetic moment

In non-magnetic materials: electron magnetic moments are randomly oriented → cancel each other → no net magnetism

Alignment of atomic magnetic moments → aligned domains → material becomes magnet

TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.q: Define ore and give 3 examples with their chemical formulas. Explain concentration of ore.
TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.solution:
Ore: A naturally occurring mineral deposit from which a metal can be extracted economically.

Examples:
1. Bauxite (Al₂O₃·2H₂O) - ore of aluminum
2. Hematite (Fe₂O₃) - ore of iron
3. Chalcopyrite (CuFeS₂) - ore of copper

Concentration of ore: Process of removing unwanted impurities (gangue) from ore to increase metal content.

Methods:
1. Gravity separation (different densities)
2. Magnetic separation (magnetic property difference)
3. Froth flotation (wetting properties difference)

TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.q: Explain the difference between roasting and calcination with suitable examples.
TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.solution:
Roasting:
• Ore heated strongly in presence of air/oxygen
• Converts ore to oxide
• Example: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂
• Used for sulfide ores (galena, chalcopyrite, sphalerite)

Calcination:
• Ore heated strongly in absence of air/limited oxygen
• Decomposes ore by heat
• Example: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
• Used for carbonate ores (limestone, dolomite) and hydroxide ores (bauxite)

Key difference: Roasting requires oxygen; calcination requires absence of oxygen

TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.q: Describe the extraction of iron from hematite ore using blast furnace. Name the three zones.
TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.solution:
Blast Furnace has three zones:

1. Combustion Zone (bottom, 1500°C): Coke burns in air → C + O₂ → CO₂ + heat

2. Reduction Zone (middle, 800-1200°C): Iron oxide reduced → Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂

3. Fusion Zone (upper): Limestone (CaCO₃) decomposes → CaO + CO₂. CaO combines with impurities (silica) → slag (CaSiO₃) separates from molten iron

Output: Molten iron (pig iron) at bottom; slag floats on top

Overall: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂

TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.q: What is the reactivity series? Explain how it helps in metal extraction.
TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.solution:
Reactivity series: An arrangement of metals in decreasing order of their reactivity (tendency to lose electrons).

Order (most to least reactive): K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Ni > Sn > Pb > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au

Application in metal extraction:
1. Highly reactive metals (K, Na): Extracted by electrolysis of molten compounds
2. Moderately reactive metals (Al, Mg, Zn): Extracted by electrolysis or carbon reduction
3. Less reactive metals (Fe, Cu): Extracted by carbon/CO reduction
4. Least reactive metals (Ag, Au): Found free in nature; simple purification needed

Rule: Metal higher in series can displace metal lower in series from its salt

TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.q: Explain the process of refining crude iron into steel. What are the main impurities removed?
TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.solution:
Refining crude iron (pig iron) into steel:

Process (Bessemer or Open Hearth method):
Step 1: Molten pig iron heated in furnace
Step 2: Air blown through molten iron → oxygen reacts with impurities
Step 3: Carbon oxidized: C + O₂ → CO₂ (removes excess carbon)
Step 4: Phosphorus oxidized: 4P + 5O₂ → 2P₂O₅
Step 5: Silicon oxidized: Si + O₂ → SiO₂
Step 6: Lime (CaO) added → forms slag with oxides
Step 7: Slag removed; refined steel remains

Main impurities removed: Carbon, phosphorus, silicon, sulfur

Result: Steel (iron + 0.1-1.5% carbon) with desired properties

TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.q: What is an alloy? Give 3 examples with their composition and uses.
TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.solution:
Alloy: A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal with non-metal.

Examples:

1. Steel (Fe + C, 0.1-1.5%):
   Uses: Tools, machines, structures, vehicles

2. Brass (Cu + Zn, 60% Cu + 40% Zn):
   Uses: Decorative items, pipes, cartridge cases

3. Bronze (Cu + Sn, 88% Cu + 12% Sn):
   Uses: Sculptures, coins, bells, bearings

Advantages of alloys over pure metals:
• Greater hardness and strength
• Better corrosion resistance
• Lower melting point
• Enhanced appearance

TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.q: Describe the electroplating process with diagram description. Why is zinc plated on iron?
TS::10::Science::principles-of-metallurg.solution:
Electroplating: Coating one metal with another using electrical current.

Setup:
• Anode: Metal to be deposited (e.g., zinc)
• Cathode: Object to be plated (e.g., iron)
• Electrolyte: Salt solution of plating metal (ZnSO₄)
• Power source: Battery/DC source

Process:
• Positive terminal → Anode (zinc) → electrons removed → Zn → Zn²⁺
• Zn²⁺ migrate to cathode through electrolyte
• Cathode (iron): Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn deposited on iron surface

Why zinc on iron:
1. Zinc is more reactive than iron
2. Zinc oxidizes preferentially → protects iron from rusting (sacrificial protection)
3. Zinc coating is hard, attractive, resistant to corrosion

TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.q: Explain why carbon forms covalent bonds and write electron dot structure for methane (CH₄).
TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.solution:
Why carbon forms covalent bonds:
• Carbon has 4 valence electrons (electron configuration 2,4)
• Requires 4 more electrons to complete octet
• Cannot lose/gain 4 electrons (would require high energy)
• Forms 4 covalent bonds by sharing electrons

Electron dot structure of methane (CH₄):
        H
        |
    H—C—H
        |
        H

Each line represents shared pair (covalent bond)
Carbon shares one electron with each hydrogen
All atoms achieve noble gas configuration (C gets 8e⁻, H gets 2e⁻)

TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.q: Define saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons with examples. Explain their difference.
TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.solution:
Saturated hydrocarbon: Hydrocarbon with only single bonds (C-C and C-H).
Examples: Methane (CH₄), Ethane (C₂H₆), Propane (C₃H₈)
General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
Properties: Less reactive, lower density, stable

Unsaturated hydrocarbon: Hydrocarbon with one or more double/triple bonds (C=C or C≡C).
Examples: Ethene (C₂H₄), Ethyne (C₂H₂), Benzene (C₆H₆)
Formula: CₙH₂ₙ (alkenes), CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (alkynes)
Properties: More reactive, can undergo addition reactions, decolorizes bromine/KMnO₄

Key difference: Saturation with hydrogen determines reactivity

TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.q: What are functional groups? List 5 functional groups with their structure and class of compound.
TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.solution:
Functional group: Atom or group of atoms responsible for chemical properties of organic compound.

Five functional groups:

1. Hydroxyl (-OH): Class = Alcohol; Example = C₂H₅OH (ethanol)
2. Carbonyl (C=O): Class = Aldehyde/Ketone; Example = CH₃CHO (acetaldehyde)
3. Carboxyl (-COOH): Class = Carboxylic acid; Example = CH₃COOH (acetic acid)
4. Amino (-NH₂): Class = Amine; Example = C₂H₅NH₂ (ethylamine)
5. Ether (-O-): Class = Ether; Example = C₂H₅OC₂H₅ (diethyl ether)

Same functional group → similar chemical reactions in different compounds

TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.q: Write the structures and properties of ethane and ethene. Why is ethene more reactive?
TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.solution:
Ethane (C₂H₆) - Saturated:
Structure: H-C-C-H (with 3 H on each C)
           |   |
Properties: Single C-C bond, least reactive, burns in air, no color

Ethene (C₂H₄) - Unsaturated:
Structure: H   H
           | = |
           C   C
           | | (double bond between carbons)
Properties: Double C=C bond, more reactive, burns with black smoke, decolorizes bromine solution

Why ethene is more reactive:
1. Double bond (C=C) is stronger than single bond (C-C) → easier to break
2. π-electrons in double bond are exposed → more available for reaction
3. Addition reactions: C=C + X₂ → C-X bonds form
4. Example: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ (1,2-dibromoethane)

TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.q: Explain homologous series with properties. Write the homologous series of alkanes up to C₄.
TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.solution:
Homologous series: Group of compounds with same general formula, differing by CH₂ unit, showing gradation in properties.

Properties of homologous series:
1. Each member differs by CH₂ unit
2. Same general formula (e.g., CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ for alkanes)
3. Similar chemical properties
4. Gradation in physical properties (melting point, boiling point, density)
5. Successive members differ by 14 in molecular weight

Alkane homologous series (up to C₄):
1. Methane: CH₄ (M = 16)
2. Ethane: C₂H₆ (M = 30)
3. Propane: C₃H₈ (M = 44)
4. Butane: C₄H₁₀ (M = 58)

Boiling points increase: CH₄ (-161°C) → C₂H₆ (-89°C) → C₃H₈ (-42°C) → C₄H₁₀ (-0.5°C)

TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.q: What is addition reaction? Explain with example of ethene reacting with hydrogen and bromine.
TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.solution:
Addition reaction: Reaction where atoms or groups add across double/triple bonds in unsaturated compounds.

Conditions: Double/triple bonds present; no atoms removed from molecule

Example 1 - Hydrogenation of ethene:
C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ (ethane)
Condition: Nickel catalyst, heat (~150°C)
Product: Saturated compound formed
Use: Converting vegetable oils (unsaturated) to ghee/butter (saturated)

Example 2 - Halogenation of ethene:
C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ (1,2-dibromoethane)
Condition: Room temperature, dark
Observation: Reddish-brown bromine solution decolorizes
Mechanism: Br-Br bond breaks, each Br adds to carbons of C=C bond

TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.q: Describe the structure of benzene. Explain why benzene is less reactive than alkenes despite having three C=C bonds.
TS::10::Science::carbon-and-its-compound.solution:
Structure of benzene (C₆H₆):
• Hexagonal ring of 6 carbons
• Each carbon bonded to one hydrogen
• Alternating single and double C-C bonds (actually resonance hybrid)
• Can be represented as two structures resonating:
  Structure 1: C=C-C=C-C=C (alternate double bonds)
  Structure 2: C-C=C-C=C-C (shifted double bonds)
• Actual structure: Hybrid with equal C-C bond order (1.5)

Why benzene is less reactive than alkenes:
1. π-electrons in benzene are delocalized over entire ring (resonance stabilization)
